Hidden ecosystem: Scientists discover 245 animals living inside a single deep-sea rock

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1086 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, deep beneath the Pacific Ocean, scientists have uncovered a surprising world of tiny animals living inside metal-rich rocks that take millions of years to form.
  • Although they may look like ordinary stones, these nodules offer something unusual in the deep ocean.
  • Polymetallic nodules are dark, roughly fist-sized formations made largely of iron and manganese oxides.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, deep beneath the Pacific Ocean, scientists have uncovered a surprising world of tiny animals living inside metal-rich rocks that take millions of years to form. These rocks, known as polymetallic nodules, contain miniature cracks and cavities that provide shelter for creatures smaller than a millimeter.

Although they may look like ordinary stones, these nodules offer something unusual in the deep ocean. They create hard surfaces in an environment dominated by soft mud, while their internal spaces provide additional habitats for marine life.

Polymetallic nodules are dark, roughly fist-sized formations made largely of iron and manganese oxides. They grow at an extraordinarily slow pace, often adding only a few millimeters over a million years. Found at ocean depths ranging from 4,000 to 6,000 meters, they can remain on the seafloor for millions of years.

Researchers set out to investigate the tiny organisms living within these ancient formations and determine how important the nodules are to deep-sea biodiversity.

Recent findings suggest that dr. Tanja Stratmann, a deep-sea ecologist and one of the study's three lead authors, explains: "In our study we show that the sizes of cracks inside the nodules are large enough to provide home to animals that are smaller than a millimeter in size.".

Hundreds of Tiny Animals Found Inside a Single Rock.

To explore these hidden habitats, the research team collected nodules from the Clarion-Clipperton Zone, a vast region of the central Pacific Ocean. They used specialized sampling equipment, including box corers that collect sections of the seafloor and remotely operated diving robots capable of working at extreme depths.

Back in the laboratory, the researchers carefully opened the nodules and extracted the tiny animals concealed within their cracks and crevices.

The results revealed an unexpectedly rich community of marine life. Across 244 nodules, the team identified 4,139 individual animals. Each nodule contained an average of 17 animals, but one particularly crowded specimen sheltered an astonishing 245 individuals.

It has been revealed that the discovery reveals that these rocks are more than simple surfaces where marine organisms can attach themselves. Their intricate internal structures create three-dimensional living spaces, allowing animals to inhabit protected areas within the nodules themselves.

It has been revealed that dr. Coral Diaz-Recio Lorenzo explains: "The crevices in the polymetallic nodules function as small shelters and provide home to animals that we do not encounter in the soft sediment of the seafloor.".

Hidden Ecosystems Unlike Those on the Surrounding Seafloor.

Although the nodules contained fewer animals than the surrounding muddy sediment, their contribution to deep-sea life was still substantial.

Recent findings suggest that for roundworms (nematodes), the number living inside the nodules amounted to approximately 10% of the number found in the surrounding sediment. For tiny crustaceans (copepods), the figure was about 25%.

According to recent reports, however, the most crucial finding was not simply how many animals the researchers discovered. It was how different the communities inside the rocks were from those living in the nearby mud.

It has been revealed that genetic analyses revealed that the animals inhabiting the nodules formed distinctive communities. Remarkably, these communities remained highly similar across locations separated by large distances (up to 1,000 km), even though they differed significantly from the organisms found in the surrounding seafloor sediment.

Recent findings suggest that this suggests that polymetallic nodules support specialized habitats that are not easily replaced by other parts of the deep ocean. Their cracks and cavities offer living conditions that certain organisms appear to depend on.

Deep-Sea Mining Could Destroy These Ancient Habitats.

The findings raise serious concerns about the potential environmental consequences of deep-sea mining.

Polymetallic nodules contain economically valuable metals, including nickel, cobalt, and copper. These resources have attracted interest in industrial mining operations that would collect the nodules directly from the ocean floor.

However, removing the rocks would also eliminate the miniature habitats they contain, along with the animals living inside them.

Recent findings suggest that one example is Thurammina sp. 1, a single-celled organism found particularly frequently within the nodules. This species appears especially well adapted to the sheltered spaces inside the rocks, making it an example of the specialized life that could be threatened by their removal.

The problem is that these habitats cannot quickly recover. Because polymetallic nodules require millions of years to develop, new ones would not form within a human lifetime. Mining could therefore eliminate ecosystems that would take geological timescales to replace.

Prof. Sabine Gollner warns: "Our findings point out that commercial mining may result in an irreversible loss of undescribed and unique biodiversity associated to nodules. This needs to be considered in environmental management of deep-sea mining.".

Scientists Race to Understand What Could Be Lost.

The discovery highlights an often overlooked aspect of ocean conservation. Protecting deep-sea ecosystems requires more than safeguarding large, visible animals. It also means considering the microscopic and nearly microscopic organisms that inhabit specialized environments hidden within the seafloor.

An notable question remains unanswered: If deep-sea mining destroys these nodule communities, could some species disappear entirely?

Recent findings suggest that researchers still need to determine whether organisms that depend on the nodules also inhabit other parts of the ocean. If certain species are restricted to these habitats, removing the nodules could potentially contribute to their global extinction.

Understanding where these animals live and how widely they are distributed will be essential for identifying areas that need protection and evaluating the potential ecological damage caused by deep-sea mining.

To investigate further, Dr. Tanja Stratmann is presently participating in an international research expedition to the Clarion-Clipperton Zone, where scientists are continuing to study the ecosystems associated with polymetallic nodules.

This expedition and other follow-up investigations are independently funded through the JPIOcean projects MiningImpact 2 and 3.

Industry observers note that the findings reveal that even a single rock on the deep ocean floor can support a surprisingly complex community of life. As interest in harvesting the ocean's mineral resources grows, scientists are working to understand these hidden ecosystems before habitats that took millions of years to form are permanently lost.

Industry observers note that if three seasons of Yellowjackets has taught us anything, it's that you don't mess with Shauna Shipman (aka Shauna Sadecki). Melissa learned that the hard way last season, when she sent a tape that put the Yellowjackets on her scent.

Shauna (Melanie Lynskey) didn't just find her, attack her, and bite off a bit of Melissa's arm. She also tried to feed it to her. Well, Season 4 of Yellowjackets came back with a vengeance, and so did Melissa (Hillary Swank).

According to recent reports, melissa notes she "rebooted her life" — which is a wild way to reframe faking your death. "I'm still the same person you married," she insists, "just with a different name and way, way shittier past than I told you about on our first date.".

Then this conversation reveals something huge:.

Sources indicate that melissa goes on to say that it was because she wish she'd known Hannah that she moved to the late scientist's hometown to start over. "Maybe I could create a life in her honor," she says. That might be true. But even as Melissa comes clean, she's still lying to Alex. In a recent development, the episode begins with the Yellowjackets in a Canadian hospital, seeing their injuries tended to. But there's no sign of Hannah.

As the Yellowjackets share their story of survival with authorities, they all recite the exact same story:.

According to recent reports, "The plane crashed. Our friends died. And the rest of starved and scavenged and prayed until they finally found us.".

Industry observers note that they claim to have no knowledge of the missing frog scientists. To cover their tracks, they let the adults assume Hannah made the distress call. So, Natalie (Sophie Thatcher) never gets proper credit for her heroics there.

How Hannah died, however, is still a mystery.

It has been revealed that after the scene of Melissa's confession to her wife, a title card states four weeks have passed. Shauna is acting out in her frustration, lashing out at a convenience store clerk and a stinky detective, the latter of whom has lost any trace of Melissa and her family.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • Marjorie Taylor Greene of Georgia spoke at a white nationalist event organized by Holocaust denier Nick Fuentes that caused Republican leaders to denounce her.
  • Last week, Greene’s Twitter account was temporarily suspended by the Elon Musk-headed platform over a tweet with a graphic referring to a “Trans Day of Vengeance,” as she denounced a planned transgender rights rally.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Editor’s Note:  Dean Obeidallah, a former attorney, is the host of SiriusXM radio’s daily program “The Dean Obeidallah Show.” Follow him @DeanObeidallah@masto.ai. The opinions expressed in this commentary are his own. View more opinion on CNN.

Last year, GOP Rep. Marjorie Taylor Greene of Georgia spoke at a white nationalist event organized by Holocaust denier Nick Fuentes that caused Republican leaders to denounce her.

Last week, Greene’s Twitter account was temporarily suspended by the Elon Musk-headed platform over a tweet with a graphic referring to a “Trans Day of Vengeance,” as she denounced a planned transgender rights rally.

And come Tuesday, Greene has announced plans to protest in Latest York City when former President Donald Trump is expected to be arraigned on an indictment of more than 30 counts, calling the proceedings against him an “unconstitutional WITCH HUNT!”.

Sources indicate that but on Sunday, Greene was featured on CBS’ “60 Minutes” in an interview the long-running show promoted on Twitter with the tease: “Republican Rep. Marjorie Taylor Greene, nicknamed MTG, isn’t afraid to share her opinions, no matter how intense and in-your-face they are. She sits down with Lesley Stahl this Sunday on 60 Minutes.” The images attached to this tweet by “60 Minutes” include Greene and Stahl walking through the US Capitol, taking a stroll outside and Greene showing Stahl something on her phone.

It's time for Marjorie Taylor Greene to go.

In the segment that aired Sunday night, Stahl noted the congresswoman had moved from the fringe to the GOP’s front row in two years despite a “sharp tongue” and “some pretty radical views” as well as “over the top” comments such as “the Democrats are a party of pedophiles.” Stahl also referred to video of Greene chasing a Parkland, Florida, school shooting survivor, still maintaining that the 2020 election was stolen and failing to criticize Trump over spending. (The interview was conducted before news of his indictment.).

But Stahl didn’t mention Greene spoke at a white nationalist event a year ago while a member of Congress or her extreme anti-Muslim views and her defense of January 6 rioters.

Criticism of CBS for amplifying Greene has been swift and well-deserved even before the program aired. Former GOP Rep. Adam Kinzinger of Illinois tweeted beforehand: “Wow. Insane that 60 min would do this.” (Kinzinger is a CNN senior political commentator.).

Journalist Molly Jong-Fast also slammed “60 Minutes” with the tweet: “Attention is currency and 60 minutes is spending its currency on the Jewish space lasers woman.” (Jong-Fast was apparently referring to Greene’s past claim that a massive California wildfire was started by “a laser” beamed from space controlled by a prominent Jewish banking family.).

David Hogg, who survived the 2018 horrific school shooting at Marjory Stoneman Douglas High School in Parkland and has since become an activist against gun violence, responded, “I look forward to your questions about why she thinks school shootings are fake and why she’s supported QAnon.”.

Trump's risky call for protests.

Greene amplified the conspiracy theory — two years before being elected to Congress — that the Parkland shooting that took 17 lives was staged. And in 2019, Greene appeared on video confronting Hogg outside the Capitol when he was championing laws to save lives from gun violence, screaming that the then-teenager was a “coward.” She also called Hogg “#littleHitler” on social media.

Greene’s own tweet promoting Sunday’s segment was not filled with her typical smears of “fake news” when she doesn’t like the coverage. Rather, Greene urged people to tune in as she praised “60 Minutes” host Stahl (and misspelled her first name): “It was an honor to spend a few days with the legendary icon Leslie Stahl and talented crew @60Minutes.” Greene added, “Leslie is a trailblazer for women in journalism. And while we may disagree on some issues, I respect her greatly.”.

It has been revealed that now, it is true that “60 Minutes” over its 50-plus-year history has featured what the show has dubbed “controversial” guests. These include a 2000 interview with Oklahoma City bomber Timothy McVeigh, whose 1995 terrorist attack left 168 dead, including 19 children. And the show did a 1979 interview with Iran’s Ayatollah Ruhollah Khomeini.

It has been revealed that perhaps “60 Minutes” views Greene — who has repeatedly downplayed and even defended the January 6, 2021, attack plus called for the GOP to become the party of “Christian nationalism” — in the vein of its long list of controversial guests. (CBS had not responded to a request from CNN for comment at time of publishing.).

Join us on Twitter and Facebook.

Recent findings suggest that however, the choice of Greene as a guest instantly recalls the comments of then-CBS CEO Les Moonves during Trump’s 2016 presidential campaign when he admitted that Trump’s candidacy “may not be good for America, but it’s damn good for CBS.” Moonves added, “The money’s rolling in and this is fun. … (T)his is going to be a very good year for us,” concluding, “Sorry. It’s a terrible thing to say. But bring it on, Donald. Keep going.”.

Moonves may be gone from CBS, but it appears his mindset continues at “60 Minutes.” And that may be good for “60 Minutes,” but it’s definitely not good for America.

Industry News: How This Year’s Movies From ‘Artificial’ to ‘I Play Rocky’ Turn Political Anxiety Into Compelling Stories

📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1501 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Variety

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read

According to recent reports, for years, Simon Rich wanted to sound the alarm about AI.Rich’s childhood friend Dan Selsam worked as a researcher at OpenAI; Selsam showed Rich, a writer known for humorous essays and for the film “An American Pickle,” an early version of the software, and the two friends discussed its ramifications.“It seemed to have real contempt for mankind,” Rich says. “It scared the hell out of me.” Rich published a book, “which was completely ignored,” and found himself striking out in his attempts to get attention with magazine articles. “So, in desperation,” he recalls, “I was like, ‘Maybe if I got a movie star…’”He got Andrew Garfield. In “Artificial,” Garfield plays OpenAI CEO Sam Altman as a blithely destructive sociopath who manipulates his way into the center of a potentially civilization-ending technological advance. Rich uses the juicy character to tell a story about the most consequential political problem of the present moment.“I’ve been living with knowledge of this danger for at least five years, due to my fluke friendship with this scientist,” he says. (Selsam issued a public warning about AI’s increasingly uncontrollable behavior in September.) “I wrote this film out of a desperation to communicate to the world this information.”That desperation may be unique to Rich. But the desire to use the tools of screenwriting to illuminate political concerns is certainly not. Had “Artificial” simply been an enumeration of AI’s dangers, it’d likely have attracted as much attention as Rich’s book; instead, it’s a well-told story with a sharp argument at its core. That makes it one of several movies this year that use character and incident — the stuff of quality storytelling — to illuminate their writers’ very real political concerns.That goes for the year’s most-discussed blockbusters: Writer-director Christopher Nolan has imbued “The Odyssey” with a rueful sense of what it means to lose one’s humanity in wartime, while, if it’s anything like its two predecessor films, “Dune: Part Three,” written by Denis Villeneuve and Brian K. Vaughan, promises to examine the uses, and misuses, of power.But it’s showing up across more human-scale dramas this fall, as well. Take “I Play Rocky.” The film depicts the writing and production of “Rocky,” which — before it was an Oscar-winning smash — was the Hail Mary attempt of unknown actor Sylvester Stallone (played by Anthony Ippolito) to write himself a place in the industry. For screenwriter Peter Gamble, the story has resonances well beyond Hollywood history.“‘Rocky’ came out right after the Vietnam War, and it was a time when people needed to believe,” Gamble says. Stallone, in the film’s telling, is the ultimate underdog; Gamble, who himself yearned for a screenwriting breakout, could relate. The message of the film, the writer says, is intended in part for his children: “They’re like, ‘We’re all going to die from global warming. If not, AI is going to kill us next week.’ What power do I have in the universe at all? We need to believe in ourselves again.”American history provides many stories that feel akin to the charged atmosphere of recent years: One, as Gamble notes, is the demoralization of the Vietnam War, and another is the cataclysm of the Great Depression. “The Weight,” written by Matthew Booi and Shelby Gaines, is a rip-roaring adventure film in which unjustly imprisoned convict Samuel Murphy (Ethan Hawke) has the chance to win his freedom by transporting gold bricks across an unruly wilderness. The viewer roots for Murphy in part because he’s compellingly played by a movie star, and in part because the boot under which he struggles looks, at a moment of increased attention to mass incarceration and wealth inequality, familiar.“You don’t want it to be didactic and message-y or preachy in any way,” Gaines says. “But the idea was to try and tell a good story on a personal, individual level and hope that it would echo sympathetically with things that happen on a larger social level — both during the Great Depression and today.” Murphy’s journey depicts the stakes of its historical moment in frankly personal terms — his loss of freedom means the loss of access to his daughter, a crisis the film treats with gravity and righteous anger.“Abstraction doesn’t help you as a writer much,” Gaines says. “If you want to convey something, the heart is the place to start.”Or you can go for the gut. “Ink,” which James Graham adapted from his own stage play, makes the case that Rupert Murdoch (Guy Pearce) and newspaper editor Larry Lamb (Jack O’Connell) created the venal media world we live in today. The dawning realization that Lamb, especially, is a force for evil hits particularly hard because Graham has, in the film’s early going, taken pains to make him so charming and his exploits so rootable.“You need these people to surprise you,” Graham says, “so that you want to be in that newsroom — and suddenly, weirdly, for a brief moment, you might even want them to get one over on the establishment.” How did tabloid culture gain such purchase? Because, as the film’s characters make clear, we’re willing to pay for it.“Being Heumann” makes us root for its band of rebels, too — but, in this case, they’re working to bring about a better world. The biopic, written by Sian Heder and Rebekah Taussig, tells the story of Judith Heumann (Ruth Madeley), the activist who led the 1977 demonstration over the government’s failure to enforce disability-rights legislation. By its nature, the film is explicitly political, but its screenplay is also the product of a thoughtful, careful approach to representation and inclusivity.Taussig, who, like the late Heumann, uses a wheelchair, saw a certain power in learning about — and then writing about — the many activists Heumann helped organize. “What was so exciting about the research,” she says, “was this gold mine of learning about these absolutely compelling people.”The first-time screenwriter had grown up seeing “very little disability representation — and [when there was], it always felt so flat. There is a richness to the experience of disability that gets missed if you don’t live it and you can’t portray it.”Taussig’s ability to mine her own insights enriches the film, one that Heder, an Oscar-winner for “CODA,” intended to inspire and delight audiences, as well as educate them. “It’s very important to me that this story reach the widest audience possible,” Heder says, “because the events of the story actually were about a triumph. In a time where a lot of us are feeling really helpless, it was so important to express disabled joy and humor. I wanted to take the audience on a really entertaining ride, where they could leave seeing the world differently.”“Fjord” has a similar reframing effect — though its true-life basis is substantially more downbeat than Judith Heumann’s story. Cristian Mungiu took inspiration from the story of the Bodnariu family, an immigrant couple whose five children were taken away by the Norwegian state amid accusations of child abuse. “Fjord” presents the story of Mihai and Lisbet Gheorghiu (Sebastian Stan and Renate Reinsve) in a who-do-you-believe social drama, one with painful repercussions.“What I’m looking into, in the stories that I pick up,” Mungiu says, “is this possibility of speaking about something bigger than just that story.” For its writer-director, “Fjord” addresses the painful consequences of globalization, as people from different traditions find that they cannot in fact understand one another. “It’s not a reenactment” of the Bodnariu story, he says: “That’s the starting point of a story in which everything is structured to speak about the relationship between the majority and the individual.”“Fjord” won the top prize at this year’s Cannes; the runner-up, “Minotaur,” also places a family drama in counterpoint with a story of major import. Here, a story of marital infidelity (based on Claude Chabrol’s 1969 film “The Unfaithful Wife”) plays out in 2022 as Russia is scaling up its military actions against Ukraine.Writer-director Andrey Zvyagintsev had been working to put the film together for years — and, as he wrote, the mobilization against Ukraine was all over the news. “It was a very logical thing,” he says through a translator. “I started to fill gaps in the script with the realities of what was happening.” Like Simon Rich trying to spread the word against AI, Zvyagintsev used his script to convey what he was hearing, like local mayors asking businesspeople to choose which of their employees will be conscripted. “This is not something I took from the air,” Zvyagintsev says. “This is real information that came by phone. People would be afraid to speak up about those situations.”For Zvyagintsev, this use of character to explore the world around him is what screenwriting is all about. “The whole ocean,” he says, “can be reflected in one ocean drop.” Related Stories Celluloid Sounds: Fewer Women Composers on Screen, But Some Hit the Right Notes Robert Pattinson's 007 Movie in Talks to Shoot at Pinewood as Studio Says 'We're the Home of Bond'.

Astronomers discover a dead star spinning every 8 minutes and sending mysterious radio pulses

📅 15 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1082 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Astronomers have traced mysterious radio signals to an unusual pair of stars more than 5,000 light-years from Earth.
  • In a recent development, the discovery was made by researchers at the Curtin University branch of the International Centre for Radio Astronomy Research (ICRAR).
  • The stellar system, designated GPM J071507−114153, contains a white dwarf and a G-type star orbiting one another.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Astronomers have traced mysterious radio signals to an unusual pair of stars more than 5,000 light-years from Earth. One is a dead star that rotates every eight minutes, while its companion closely resembles our own Sun.

In a recent development, the discovery was made by researchers at the Curtin University branch of the International Centre for Radio Astronomy Research (ICRAR). Their findings reveal a previously unseen combination of stars producing radio pulses and offer fresh clues about the origins of some of the Milky Way's most puzzling signals.

The stellar system, designated GPM J071507−114153, contains a white dwarf and a G-type star orbiting one another. A white dwarf is the extremely dense remnant of a star that has exhausted its nuclear fuel and shed its outer layers. Its companion belongs to the same general category of stars as the Sun.

According to recent reports, until now, astronomers had detected similar radio pulses in systems containing white dwarfs and smaller, cooler stars known as red dwarfs. This marks the first time such signals have been identified in a system where a white dwarf orbits a Sun-like star.

A Rare Star System With Mysterious Radio Pulses.

Industry observers note that the newly identified pair belongs to an unusual group of astronomical objects called long-period transients (LPTs). These objects produce radio emissions that appear and disappear over periods lasting anywhere from several minutes to hours.

Despite growing interest in these strange signals, their origins remain poorly understood. The same ICRAR research team discovered the first known example in 2021, and only about a dozen have been identified since then.

Some of these systems contain a white dwarf alongside another star, but astronomers have struggled to determine which member of the pair is responsible for the radio emissions.

Sources indicate that the latest discovery provides an vital breakthrough. For the first time, researchers have obtained radio observations detailed enough to follow a white dwarf as it travels around its stellar companion. This allows them to pinpoint the likely location of the radio pulses much more accurately.

It has been revealed that "This is the first time the pulses are clear enough to see the white dwarf moving in its orbit around its companion, so we know that the pulsations are coming from a region close to the white dwarf, or possibly even from the white dwarf itself," said lead author Dr. Sam McSweeney.

McSweeney, now a commissioning scientist with the Square Kilometre Array Observatory, made the discovery while working at Curtin University's ICRAR branch.

To confirm the findings and examine the white dwarf's orbital motion, the researchers analyzed more than 100 hours of radio observations using computing resources at the Pawsey Supercomputing Research Centre.

Giant Magnetic Storms Detected 5,000 Light-Years Away.

Sources indicate that the radio signals revealed more than the movement of the dead star. They also gave astronomers a surprising opportunity to investigate magnetic activity on its Sun-like companion.

In a recent development, according to study co-author Associate Professor Natasha Hurley-Walker, the observations exposed stellar flares associated with powerful magnetic disturbances. Similar magnetic processes on our own Sun can lead to auroras on Earth when energetic particles interact with our planet's magnetic field and atmosphere.

The team also detected evidence that the white dwarf passed behind an especially magnetically active region near its companion.

"As a bonus, we also saw the white dwarf moving behind a region with a strong magnetic field, most likely a 'stellar prominence', which is a large loop of plasma erupting from a star's surface.".

In a recent development, A stellar prominence consists of electrically charged gas held in enormous loops by magnetic fields. These structures can extend far above a star's surface, providing clues about the powerful forces shaping its outer atmosphere.

The ability to detect such activity across thousands of light-years demonstrates how much information astronomers can extract from radio signals, even when the stars themselves are extraordinarily distant.

"It's amazing that by using radio wavelengths we can detect the storms on a star over 5000 light-years away.".

Powerful Radio Telescopes Reveal a Hidden Stellar Pair.

ICRAR researchers have played a leading role in identifying long-period transients, and the latest discovery relied on observations from several major astronomical facilities around the world.

The system was initially detected during a sweeping radio survey of the Milky Way conducted with the MWA (Murchison Widefield Array) in Western Australia.

"We detected this system in a large survey using the MWA (Murchison Widefield Array) to scan the entire Milky Way visible from Australia. We then used the MeerKAT radio telescope in South Africa to determine its precise position," said Associate Professor Hurley-Walker.

In a recent development, after the radio telescopes narrowed down the system's location, astronomers turned to the W.M. Keck Observatory on Maunakea, Hawaiʻi Island. Optical observations confirmed that the radio source was associated with a G-type star, establishing the presence of a companion similar to the Sun.

The MWA, led by Curtin University, operates at Inyarrimanha Ilgari Bundara, the CSIRO Murchison Radio-Astronomy Observatory on Wajarri Yamaji Country in Western Australia.

The MeerKAT telescope was built and is operated by the South African Radio Astronomy Observatory in South Africa's North Cape province.

According to recent reports, both instruments are precursors to the next generation of Square Kilometre Array telescopes. The Australian facility, SKA-Low, and the South African facility, SKA-Mid, are being developed to provide much greater sensitivity and detail when observing the radio universe.

For astronomers studying rare stellar systems, these future capabilities could dramatically expand the number of objects they can discover and reveal much more about the processes responsible for their unusual signals.

In a recent development, dr. McSweeney mentioned, "If we are already making such discoveries with precursor telescopes, just imagine how many more star systems we will be able to find, and what a beautifully detailed view of their signals we will have, once the SKAO telescopes are completely built.".

The findings were published in Nature Astronomy in a study titled "A long-period transient with a Sun-like companion.".

According to recent reports, materials provided by International Centre for Radio Astronomy Research. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Byrne had a literal meltdown in the most showstopping scene of Damien Chazelle’s Babylon, his career as a scene-stealing character actor has reached a upcoming high.
  • The Newly introduced Jersey native’s 2026 alone has brought eight credits, including the conclusion of his recurring character on The Boys, Coyote vs.
  • Sources indicate that in 1975, Winkler and his producing partner Robert Chartoff were developing Martin Scorsese’s Fresh York, New York at the same time as the underdog story from a then-unknown Sylvester Stallone.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Ever since P.J. Byrne had a literal meltdown in the most showstopping scene of Damien Chazelle’s Babylon, his career as a scene-stealing character actor has reached a upcoming high.

The Newly introduced Jersey native’s 2026 alone has brought eight credits, including the conclusion of his recurring character on The Boys, Coyote vs. Acme, The End of Oak Street and a series-regular role on USA’s basic cable hit The Rainmaker. Most notably, he now stars in his biggest film role to date as Oscar-winning Rocky producer Irwin Winkler in Peter Farrelly’s biographical awards contender, I Play Rocky. Related Stories Movies 'Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping' Feasting With $120M+ in Franchise's Box Office Comeback Hollywood Flashback Yo, Academy! When 'Rocky' Was Crowned Best Picture Champ.

Sources indicate that in 1975, Winkler and his producing partner Robert Chartoff were developing Martin Scorsese’s Fresh York, New York at the same time as the underdog story from a then-unknown Sylvester Stallone. The former would become the first of a half-dozen films Winkler collaborated on with Scorsese, including 2013’s The Wolf of Wall Street. It’s fitting, then, that Byrne is now playing the celebrated producer, given that his own career turning point came with his role as Rugrat in Scorsese and Leonardo DiCaprio’s unhinged take on the life of former stockbroker Jordan Belfort. (Byrne would later reunite with Scorsese on his 2016 series Vinyl.).

Byrne’s turn as a founding member of Belfort’s Stratton Oakmont is probably best remembered for one particularly rambunctious trading-floor scene in which his character shaves a female sales assistant’s head. The opportunity also allowed Byrne to put his unused finance degree from Boston College to work, albeit in a fictionalized version of a career path he had rapidly abandoned because of his aversion to boiler-room culture.

Sources indicate that in the mid-’90s, one of his Boston College professors encouraged him to try his hand at drama school instead, leading him to DePaul University in Chicago. Byrne’s time in the Windy City seems to have left a lasting impression. He often speaks about acting in the same terms that Chicago Bulls legend Michael Jordan once used to describe his record-setting 3-point barrage against the Portland Trail Blazers in Game 1 of the 1992 NBA Finals. When Byrne acts, he strives to enter a flow state, or “the zone,” as Jordan called it, where he’s so locked in to the task at hand that distractions fade and he can achieve peak performance.

Byrne’s Wolf of Wall Street video audition featured a monologue he reimagined from the ground up. Channeling his brief experience in the financial world, he portrayed his stockbroker character emotionally manipulating a widow into forking over $100,000 during a sales call. Scorsese appreciated the creative risk so much that he recited part of the speech back to Byrne during their eventual in-person callback. Byrne’s improvisational instincts and willingness to take creative leaps through punch-ups and alternative dialogue are muscles he first developed during his early days in Los Angeles.

At the turn of the century, Byrne put himself through the wringer of commercial auditions. With a talent pool far deeper than most people might expect, he knew he needed to find a way to stand out. That meant arriving with his own variations on the material or improvising in the moment. To pay the bills between sporadic acting jobs, he provided script coverage and handled other development duties at the production company of family friend and fellow Boston College alum Chris O’Donnell.

Industry observers note that eventually, he left his VP position to focus solely on acting. Nameless parts soon gave way to small but named roles, though there were milestones along the way that reinforced his greater pursuit. One came when he made Will Ferrell and Stephen Colbert laugh during a table-read scene in Nora Ephron’s Bewitched (2005). Byrne played a TV writer in the film, an early example of the showbiz-affiliated roles that would become a calling card throughout his career. He speculates that his time working in development may have influenced that pattern.

Byrne’s road to I Play Rocky can also be traced back to commercials cast by casting director Rick Montgomery. It further involved producer Toby Emmerich’s tenure as head of New Line, during which Byrne made memorable appearances in the label’s Horrible Bosses and Final Destination 5. Above all, Byrne won a major fan in Farrelly when he played a record executive in the best picture-winning Green Book, followed by Dear Santa, the Christmas comedy Farrelly co-wrote for his brother Bobby to direct.

“After Green Book, Peter was like, ‘You need your Paul Giamatti [in Sideways] part. You need a bigger part in a movie,’” Byrne tells The Hollywood Reporter.

According to recent reports, the role of Irwin Winkler still didn’t come easy. In the behind-the-scenes narrative, Winkler and Chartoff desperately want to produce Stallone’s Rocky screenplay, but he refuses to sell it unless he gets to star as the title character. Winkler and Chartoff, ever the pragmatists, try to give the aspiring young actor and screenwriter a reality check about how star power drives the financing and green-lighting of most movies. But Stallone stands his ground despite increasingly lucrative offers for the script.

Eventually, Winkler and Chartoff realize they shouldn’t be producing an underdog story about a small-time boxer named Rocky Balboa if they aren’t willing to practice what they preach. So they risk everything, including their names and their homes, to install Stallone as the star, all while distributor United Artists sets him up to fail at every turn in hopes of replacing him with a proven commodity.

Sources indicate that the casting of Byrne’s role also became rather meta because the I Play Rocky brain trust initially sought a name for Winkler. With relative unknown Anthony Ippolito already cast as young Sly, it’s understandable why they would want to shore up the surrounding roles with established, butts-in-seats actors. But the producers of I Play Rocky ultimately arrived at the same conclusion as the producers of Rocky — gamble on talent, not status.

“They wanted to get a name, because there weren’t a lot of names [in this cast]. But they were also living in the world of, If we’re going to cast Anthony Ippolito as Sylvester Stallone, then let’s give other people shots too,” Byrne says. “They all knew me from these small parts. Then they just believed in me enough to give me a shot. I want to tell the world that there’s honestly no small parts. Someone will ultimately give you a chance.”.

It has been revealed that below, in a conversation with THR, Byrne also discusses the day his improvisational skills resulted in I Play Rocky’s most hilarious scene. He also addresses whether the strained relationship between Winkler and Stallone in recent years influenced his take at all.

Recent findings suggest that it’s not talent. I just have three children. I have to pay for their lives. That’s all that is. It’s like, Yes, I’ll do that. I have three children.

You’ve still cemented yourself as one of the industry’s go-to character actors.

Can you feel that wind in your sail?

It has been revealed that I always say ABC: always be classy. So I don’t know if I can admit to that, but I do have repeat buyers, if you will, because they’re buddies. Once I work on anything, I tend to have repeat business. So I’ll meet you halfway. I hate giving myself flowers like that, but I believe in myself to deliver. And if other people see that, then I appreciate it.

When you hear labels like “character actor” or “comic relief” or “scene-stealer,” do you bristle at all? Or do you embrace the lane you’ve carved out for yourself?

It has been revealed that it’s funny. I don’t even look at it that way. All ships rise with the tide. I want everyone to score and win. I’m always surrounded by incredible actors in everything I do, so everyone passes the ball nicely. It’s not about being funny or stealing scenes. It’s, How do I make these moments pop more? This sounds so cheesy and trite, but it’s really, How do I service the director or the writer? I’ve been doing this so long that they are often my really good friends.

Industry observers note that when someone makes a movie, they’ve put four years of their life into it. They’ve battled producers and studio executives to get this one day of this particular scene, and half their budget is being spent on a goddamn crane shot. So I just want to do everything I can for them. I put in the work, and my brain just naturally looks for moments that can pop. Is there an ability to make this zeitgeisty so that people can relate to it and it can become its own thing?

Where did this mentality come from?

I started out in Los Angeles doing commercials, and I was baptized by fire doing them. Commercials are like street basketball. It’s rough. They’re not nice to you. The rooms aren’t sweet. They’re not kind. But some of the best actors are commercial actors. They just never found the right lane or the right agent. They’re still out there, and they’re extraordinary actors. But adding jokes during commercial auditions is how I trained my brain to find moments to pop. I would think of the fifth funniest joke in my brain because the first four would probably be thought of by someone else.

Recent findings suggest that that mindset succeeds in scenarios where I have fearless directors who’ve proven themselves. It’s usually the great directors like Marty Scorsese or Peter Farrelly or Damien Chazelle who don’t have to worry about notes from everyone. They know I’ve done the work and have their vision in mind, so they’ll take the handcuffs off me. They’ll be like, “Just add stuff. We trust you. Go.” They know that before a job, I’ll literally sit in a hotel room for two weeks and have food sent up while I make sure I’m doing everything I can for them. I don’t want to let anyone down.

Recent findings suggest that you’re also asked to play showbiz people fairly often. The Boys, Babylon, The Big Cigar and A Complete Unknown are only a few examples, as is your current role as Irwin Winkler in I Play Rocky. Do you have any theories why this has become your niche?

I feel like I have a face like that. I also do a lot of period pieces and play a lot of lawyers. That’s just what’s filming now. But I think it’s all because I know those characters well from when I started out in Los Angeles.

I owe a lot to Chris O’Donnell. When he was Robin [in Batman & Robin], he had a production company at Warner Bros. His sisters and my sister are really good friends. And because I had a finance degree from Boston College, I was like, If acting doesn’t work out, I can be an intern with them. To his credit, his company gave me a script and were like, “Hey, do coverage on this script.” So I did, and the coverage was called “brilliant.” But it was only brilliant because I literally just went to grad school where I learned arc and character. I literally just wrote papers for three years.

Chris was like, “Be our story editor.” And I was like, “Chris, I came here to act.” Then he gave me the greatest gift ever when he noted, “No, come and go as you please.” So I was able to walk onto the Warner Bros. and work for him, while also doing commercials and small TV jobs. Every time I tried to quit, they were like, “You’re a vice president right now.”.

I set up movies. I learned the business. I would walk past The West Wing and ER stages, and I told myself that I wouldn’t set foot on those stages until I was invited. And I did eventually book those jobs. So I became comfortable being in that environment, and it wasn’t so daunting going into those rooms.

Sources indicate that it’s because of all those early experiences that I have a lot of friends who are producers, writers and directors. So I know this world well, and when someone says, “Play this showbiz part,” I’m like, “Trust me, I got it.”.

You worked with Peter Farrelly on Green Book and Dear Santa. Did he go straight to you for Irwin Winkler?

It wasn’t straight to me, but I love Peter forever. I want to tell the world that there’s honestly no small parts, and you never know what’s going to come around. And that’s why this movie was so super meta for me. They wanted to get a name, because there weren’t a lot of names [in this cast]. But they were also living in the world of, If we’re going to cast Anthony Ippolito as Sylvester Stallone, then let’s give other people shots too.

It has been revealed that after Green Book, Peter was like, “You need your Paul Giamatti [in Sideways] part. You need a bigger part in a movie.” [I Play Rocky casting director] Rick Montgomery cast me in commercials years ago, and [producer] Toby Emmerich also ran New Line when I had small parts in Horrible Bosses and Final Destination 5.

Industry observers note that so they all knew me from these small parts, and they all said, “He’s ready to have a bigger part. Come audition for this.” Then they just believed in me enough to give me a shot. Someone will ultimately give you a chance, just like they once gave it to Sylvester Stallone and now Anthony Ippolito and me.

Everything is driven by the same dozen names now, so it’s nice to hear that Farrelly is looking elsewhere.

According to recent reports, yeah, he’s incredibly loyal. If you look at his movies, the same people always come back. When you go out for drinks with Pete, 32 people show up with him. I love that idea of a family. Working with friends is the best way to go to work, and that’s another reason why I get repeat business.

When it’s four in the morning on a Friday night and you’ve been shooting 12 hours, we’re still cheerleaders for each other. I love those kinds of sets. It kills me when I see people being cancers or want to get off set. Again, I know what my friend went through to be here after four years. So I always say, “Let’s deliver this moment the best way we can because we’re never coming back.”.

What went through your mind when you first witnessed Anthony Ippolito’s take on Sly?

It was at a table read, and while everybody does a version of Sylvester Stallone, I was like, We’re living and dying on this kid. This is the moment. And as soon as he opened his mouth, it was so subtle and soulful and full of heart. It honestly surpassed what my expectation was going to be. I have been doing this a long time, and this is the biggest part I’ve ever gotten in a movie. It’s so beautiful for me, personally. But I can’t help but get so psyched for this kid because he’s so spectacular.

I’ve been around some incredible performances. I watched Leo just destroy on The Wolf of Wall Street. And Margot Robbie, I still wish she got her flowers for Babylon. There’s even a scene with me and Laura Dern on Big Little Lies. When you’re an actor in a scene with them and the camera’s not on you, there’s just a moment when you become an audience member. And you’re like, Oh shit, it’s happening. You can feel it in the room and you want to deliver for them and be there for them. And that’s what happened with Anthony.

Recent findings suggest that he was in the zone. That’s what basketball players say when the net looks like the size of an ocean and they can’t miss. That’s what it felt like watching Anthony. He was so good that I kept thinking, Did Sylvester Stallone travel through space and time to possess this kid’s body? That’s how special it was. Then Pete would call cut, and Anthony would come back online and say, “Hey, what are we getting for dinner tonight?” And I was just like, “What is going on right now?” Peter and I were like, “Is he the world’s greatest actor?” He also played Rocky and Sylvester Stallone, and it was just crazy to watch him play two different characters.

I also watched Timothée Chalamet be Bob Dylan, and that was another time where I was like, “Holy shit.” But Timmy would stay in character, unlike Anthony. So everyone has their own method, and there is no right way.

There’s no love lost between Stallone and Winkler in recent years. Sly resents the fact that Winkler retains full ownership of the Rocky franchise and that he doesn’t have a piece of the pie to leave for his family. Did you and Farrelly ever discuss planting that seed of acrimony for where their relationship would end up?

Producers are observers. They are there to eliminate risk, put out fires and make sure that the art happens. Sometimes, they have to guide it and have their influence, but that’s what they are. Bob Chartoff and Irwin Winkler were the greatest producers and the ultimate backstop to any ball getting past the catcher. So that’s what I had to deal with in my role.

In a recent development, the first time you meet my character, he’s all business. He’s not mean to Sly, but he just doesn’t look the part for the role being cast. But then he’s intrigued by this smart guy sitting in front of him, and then they eventually read his scripts to see that there’s talent there. At first, Winkler believes in the project, and then he learns to believe in the person behind it.

Sources indicate that the end of the movie demonstrates the real-life clip of when Rocky won best picture at the 1977 Oscars. Bob Chartoff and Irwin Winkler stood up, and Irwin Winkler immediately grabbed Sylvester Stallone to join them on stage, which is rare. It’s usually just the producers who accept the best picture award.

Industry observers note that but Winkler grabbed Sylvester Stallone and put his arm around him with such love. It was like, This is my son. I believe in you so much. I mortgaged my house for you. I didn’t just bet on a movie. I bet on a child that I love. It’s the idea that you would do anything for your kids, and like I stated, I literally work for my children. The money comes in the door, and it goes right to give them every opportunity to succeed in life.

According to recent reports, whatever the extraneous stuff is between them now, I was meant to portray that period of time in the late ‘70s. I was there to share the message that if you really fucking do the work and you believe in yourself — and then you surround yourself with like-minded people who truly believe in you as well — then anything is possible. Maybe you too will one day win an Oscar. That was a special moment in all of their lives, and that’s what I needed to play and had to play.

In a perfect world, a clause would kick in after x amount of years so that the original creator receives at least a sliver of the pie. But like you remarked, Winkler and Chartoff risked their homes on a complete unknown. They also gave him profit participation on the first film, as well as most, if not all, of the future films. So I hate to both-sides the issue, but I really do see both sides here.

It has been revealed that of course, I thought about all of that and who these people are today and yesterday. But my job was to play that moment in time in which greatness happened. It was a beautiful thing, even if you’re always battling for what you want and going at it. That’s why I have that moment after Winkler found out that Sly and Carl Weathers had never boxed before.

According to recent reports, yeah, Winkler went out and got the world’s greatest boxing choreographer, but then Sly kicked him out. All the script had was Winkler saying, “It’s a boxing movie!” So I mentioned to Peter, “The producer’s job is to put out fires, so he would lose his mind right now. This is a handcuffs-off moment. Let me riff and play a little bit here.” It was a scary moment because it was late at night right before Thanksgiving, and everybody wanted to go home for Thanksgiving. But here I was adding a lot to the scene.

It has been revealed that to Peter’s credit, he let me go. I made that line up about The Godfather: “It’s not about the mafia. It’s about a nice Italian family that loves pasta.” Then, because he’s angry, he has to get the fuck out of the room. So I went up the stairs toward the door, and I added the lines about how this “happens to be” a set of stairs and how this “happens to be” a door as he walks out. So you do go at it when you’re making films because you’re passionate about the product.

Yeah, the “happens to be” scene is your “hello, college!” scene of this movie. Winkler’s meltdown is rooted in director John G. Avildsen’s position that Rocky isn’t a boxing movie. He made the point that it’s a character study about a guy who “happens to be” a boxer. Plus, it hits close to home because every entertainment journalist has written some version of that “happens to be” line about a story in which the surrounding world is incidental.

Those improvised lines came from being in the zone. It’s the best when it happens. I also didn’t know that guy was going to ask me to take off his jacket. We were just playing in the moment. They let this little chemistry experiment happen.

It has been revealed that the Rocky and Apollo fight is ultimately saved for the closing credits, serving as the punchline to the “happens to be” bit. I Play Rocky is also a character study that happens to have boxing in it.

Recent findings suggest that was that fight always intended for the credits? Or did they realize in the edit that it would make for a great gag?

Recent findings suggest that it had another great ending as well. Rocky was boxing, and when they called cut, he didn’t want to hear it. Then he was like, “I can go again.” He’d been going and going for 28 days, and then his wife came up to say, “It’s over.” And he was like, “No, no, I can do one more.”And she was like, “No, it’s over. You did it.” I could cry right now just thinking about how they ended it.

But Anthony’s earlier moment where he was hitting the door as Rocky and going, “It stinks! My life stinks!” — how were we going to top how extraordinary that was? We couldn’t top that. Showing it toward the end also has a beautiful message, so that’s moviemaking. You’re learning and adapting and changing as you’re going.

Peter also edits as he’s going, and he knows the movie so well. Like Avildsen in the movie, I would add something, and Peter would be like, “We got it. Cut. Moving on.” And I’d be like, “What do you mean you got it? I only said the line once.” And he was like, “No, no, it’s great.” This is the first movie I saw six weeks after filming it, so I remembered every second of filming. And when some of those moments came up, I was like, He was right. That is great. We didn’t need another angle.

If you had to guess, how much of Rocky did Farrelly recreate?

Sources indicate that oh God, if I was going to throw out a number, maybe 26.9 percent. I don’t know. They shot that boxing scene for a week, and that was the longest, most expensive part of the shoot.

I wish I could’ve seen Amazon’s response to it ending up in the closing credits.

(Laughs.) Again, to Peter’s credit, he mentioned, “What do we think the best part of the story is?” That’s an amazing thing. The great directors are fearless. They don’t operate from fear. They trust their instincts and their gut. They have great editors too.

Some locations probably don’t exist in the same form anymore, but for places like Rocky’s apartment, did you revisit as many original spots as possible from Rocky?

We shot at the same apartment he lived in, and it’s still a rough neighborhood to this day. We heard people around the neighborhood say, “Oh my God, this feels just like yesterday.” Some of the same people lived there 50 years ago.

Then we went to the Rocky Steps [at the Philadelphia Museum of Art], which was amazing. AnnaSophia Robb and I ran up the stairs with Anthony. Then I came back down the stairs, and Tracy Letts was there, so I have the greatest video of me and Tracy Letts running up the stairs together. I have to post it. It’s so beautiful that all these people come from around the world to run up the stairs in their gray sweatsuits. I have another little video of Anthony waiting in line to take a picture next to the statue of Rocky, dressed as Rocky.

Recent findings suggest that so it was really special to be in Philadelphia. It’s a super-duper city, man. You feel the lunch-pale vibe. We all knew how special this movie is to so many people around the world, and while Sylvester, Irwin Winkler and SteadiCam creator Garrett Brown are still alive, we didn’t want to let them down. We truly felt that way.

Overall, the movie is largely about the power of no. Sly remarked no to Winkler and Chartoff countless times before he got the deal he thought he wanted at the time. Have you had a chance to say no to something that ultimately proved to be the best decision?

My whole life is built on not understanding what the word no means. I was supposed to work on Wall Street, but then I decided to walk away to be an actor. I was told, “You can’t be an actor,” and I was like, “Yes, I can.”.

In a recent development, to me, no just means not now, and my whole life is built on that premise. Nothing is impossible. That’s why I love the movie business, and that’s what made Irwin and Bob incredible producers. They didn’t understand the word no either. If something went wrong on a film, they fixed it.

Marty Scorsese talks about this all the time [from his experiences with Winkler]. He says, “All this craziness was happening in the background, and Irwin Winkler never let me know any of it. I was just there to be free and think about the project.” So I wanted to put a little of that into I Play Rocky [when Winkler and Chartoff opt not to tell Sly they’ve mortgaged their homes to keep the movie going].

Sources indicate that I’ve always loved movies and shows about the making of famous movies or shows. Of all your other projects, is there one that would make for a compelling behind-the-scenes narrative à la I Play Rocky?

Recent findings suggest that oh, it’d be Coyote vs. Acme. My dear friend, Dave Green, directed it, and the world almost never saw it. It was going to be thrown in a vault because an accountant made a decision. We should always be art over commerce, especially when you’ve chosen to make movies for a living. I had a front row seat to what Dave went through, and he was so classy through the whole process.

Another heartbreaking aspect to the story is that [Looney Tunes character voice actor] Eric Bauza just passed away. It’s a bummer. He was a generational talent, and he was also one of the classiest, nicest guys you’ve ever met. It just kills me. He has an eight-year-old kid and a fiancée. He literally stood up for the movie while presenting at an award show and noted, “Release Coyote vs. Acme!” He said that to the corporation that paid him all his money and fed him because he voiced Looney Tunes characters.

On set, it was amazing what we did because we had no money. I wasn’t even playing that part [of Acme lawyer, Bill Pelicanos] the week before. They were like, “John Cena is going to do it. Do you want to be a sidekick?” And I was like, “Yes! I want my hair to look exactly like his, and I also want to be bald in a scene.” And they were like, “We can’t afford any of that.” And I was like, “I’m calling in favors for hair.” Everyone was doing favors for everybody on that movie. We believed in the art.

It was so meta because it was about fighting major corporations. Everyone was doing that movie for the right reason. So that would truly make for a special behind-the-scenes movie. I also just found out it can get nominated for best animated feature because over 75 percent of the project is animated. I really hope it gets its flowers.

If Babylon got the I Play Rocky treatment, what would the behind the scenes of the “hello, college!” sequence look like?

Well, we shot that 10-minute scene over three days. It was one of the greatest, most fun shooting experiences of my life because, once again, Damien let me go. I auditioned during COVID, when you couldn’t be in the room together, and I got a note back from Damien saying, “It feels like you want to really let it go.” At first, I was like, I want to stay close to the lines because this is Damien Chazelle. I’ve never auditioned for him. I love this dude. I want to be in his movie so badly.

But once he said, “Go,” I added so many horrible things. Then I handed it in, and 20 minutes later, I got the call that I got the part. When I showed up on set, I saw that the lines I had added were in the movie, and that’s when I knew I was going to riff even more. Damien ended up letting everybody play.

My close-ups were on the last day, and I had basically already lost my voice. It ended up being gone for a month. But something came out of me that day to make it all happen. When I did the first take of my close-up, they were like, “Great. That was amazing. We got it.” But I was like, “Let’s keep going. I have four more ideas. I’m going to lose my voice. I want to get it all.” We still had a game left to play, and I didn’t want to celebrate yet.

In a recent development, everybody knew how special and spectacular that scene was, and everyone was cheering for everybody when it was their take. Those special days also had moments in the zone. I was able to be conscious of how amazing this was and still deliver new stuff.

Did they actually keep the stage extra warm given the nature of the scene?

Recent findings suggest that I mean, it was hot, but that was mostly just incredible makeup. They put this gel on your head that looks like sweat. Those were three days of magic, man. Damien had a big board of all the shots he wanted, and we just checked them off as we went. It was awesome.

Industry observers note that what about The Wolf of Wall Street? How would you dramatize one of those days?

That was an amazing brotherhood. I’m still friends with so many of those guys. Jon Bernthal lived across the hall from me. Kenny Choi lived downstairs. Brian Sacca and Ethan Suplee were also close, and we had a blast. We knew how powerful that story was.

Recent findings suggest that leo sometimes likes to stay in character, but he joked, “If I stayed in character this whole time, I would have a nervous breakdown.” So we got the real Leo. We got to bro out with a buddy. He’s the man of our times. He’s the great actor. He’s charming. He’s the best storyteller. He wanted us all to have a great time. He was also producing, so he made sure that we met the real Jordan Belfort and learned how to sell from the guy. The idea was that we needed to really see who this guy is and how these people truly operate.

Industry observers note that as I mentioned earlier, the greatness of Marty is that he let us all riff and play. So I riffed with Jonah [Hill] and Leo, and that was another magical experience because I probably made up 80 percent of the lines I mentioned in that movie. Marty was always like, “It’s too clean. Mess it up. Go.”.

When I auditioned, I used my finance degree to make up my own monologue, and Marty knew it. So he memorized it and read it back to me. I was like, This is the greatest day of my life. Then, on the first day of rehearsal, Marty and Leo asked me questions about finance. I was like, I can’t believe I’m sitting here answering their finance questions. This is crazy. Am I an actor? Am I a consultant? What is happening?

Years from now, when you write your memoir, how will you sum up the 2026 chapter?

“He was the hardest working person on the set, and he was always classy.” The title of the biography should be P.J. Byrne: Over the Shoulder and Out of Focus.

There's an impostor hiding in the Hyades star cluster. Can you spot it?

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1135 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Space

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that for years I looked at Taurus and saw something perfectly sensible.
  • Industry observers note that then I discovered that Aldebaran has nothing to do with the Hyades.
  • Sources indicate that this fact exposes one of the most convincing tricks in stargazing.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that for years I looked at Taurus and saw something perfectly sensible. There was the Hyades, the big V-shaped cluster that forms the bull's face, with Aldebaran, noticeably brighter and more orange than the other stars, the dominant star. Every diagram reinforced the arrangement — Aldebaran was the eye of Taurus, the Hyades made the face, and in my head they became one object.

Industry observers note that then I discovered that Aldebaran has nothing to do with the Hyades. I remember going outside afterward and looking again, half expecting the deception to become obvious now that I knew. It didn't. Aldebaran still looked completely at home among the other stars. The difference is hidden in the one dimension our eyes judge poorly when we look into space — depth. Aldebaran is about 65 light-years away, while the Hyades are roughly 150 light-years distant. The orange eye of Taurus is a foreground star that happens to lie almost exactly along our line of sight toward the Hyades.

Sources indicate that this fact exposes one of the most convincing tricks in stargazing. The night sky looks flat, and our brains are extremely willing to believe it. But it has incredible depth — and when you can see parts of the night sky in 3D, that's when you begin to appreciate that you're not looking at a flat map. Instead, you begin to see our cosmic neighborhood as it really is. By appreciating depth, you learn its geography.

Taurus is now easy to find from the Northern Hemisphere during the evening. Once it's dark, look east for a small, tight knot of stars — the Pleiades open cluster (M45) — and then look nearby for a much larger V-shaped arrangement. That V is the Hyades, with unmistakably orange Aldebaran apparently sitting on one arm. Aldebaran's name is derived from the Arabic Al Dabarān, meaning "the follower," because it appears to trail the Pleiades across the night sky.

Recent findings suggest that the Hyades is a real physical group of stars — an open cluster — that formed together and moves through our galaxy together. About 153 light-years away, the Hyades is the nearest open star cluster to Earth. The name means "the rainmakers" because their rising and setting times in the ancient Greek sky coincided with wet weather. The stars in the Hyades are of a similar age — and mostly sun-like stars, or similar — so astronomers can tell that they all formed together in the same nebula.

Orange-red star Aldebaran — the 14th-brightest star in the night sky — is the interloper, sitting less than half as far away from the sun. If you could somehow view the neighborhood from another part of the Milky Way, the familiar arrangement would fall apart. Aldebaran would no longer sit conveniently in the bull's face, and Taurus itself would stop looking like a bull.

It has been revealed that constellations aren't objects in the same sense as a planet or star cluster. They are merely views. Even stars that appear almost side by side can be separated by enormous distances. Our entire view of the night sky is a line-of-sight, 2D phenomenon — so all the patterns we see are an illusion.

Recent findings suggest that start with Aldebaran and the Hyades using only unaided eyes. Once you have the V, remind yourself of the distances — roughly 65 light-years for Aldebaran and 150 for the Hyades — and try to imagine pulling the orange star toward you while leaving the rest of the cluster behind. Stargazing like this can be much harder than it sounds. Even the brains of seasoned stargazers are hard-wired to find patterns of stars — constellations — and they rarely practice seeing stars at their correct distances.

Binoculars are worth using for the Hyades because the cluster is broad, so low magnification suits it well. Binoculars show many additional stars, but that's not really the point. Knowing what you're looking at changes the observation more than magnification does.

Recent findings suggest that trying to see the night sky in 3D is best done one constellation at a time, but I warn you — it makes you suspicious of everything. Next time you trace Orion, Cassiopeia or Auriga, you'll always be wondering which stars are nearby and which merely look that way. Looking up the distances and working it all out for yourself is an eye-opening experience.

Learning constellations gets you around the sky in a basic sense, but learning how to dismantle them and put them back together is when you begin to know the night sky as it really is.

Sources indicate that this week is dominated by the moon. The moon is already waxing when the week begins and becomes the full Beaver Moon — a supermoon — on Nov. 24. That means progressively brighter evening skies and increasingly poor conditions for faint galaxies, nebulae and other low-contrast objects. Aldebaran and the main Hyades stars are bright enough to see from suburban skies even under strong moonlight, so you don't need to travel somewhere properly dark. Swapping your view from 2D to 3D takes only a little imagination. However, that could change in the few nights around the full moon — particularly on Nov. 23, when the waxing gibbous moon will move close to the nearby Pleiades, its strong light reducing the number of faint stars visible around them. Use binoculars to find some of its hundreds of stars.

According to recent reports, I'm a stargazer and not at all interested in Greek mythology, but it sometimes helps to know a few basic ancient myths when finding constellations. A good example is the constellation Cepheus. It's named after a king of Ethiopia, husband of Cassiopeia and father of Andromeda — all three of which are close by in the northern sky right now. Look west after dark, away from the bright moon, to find the Summer Triangle — Vega, Deneb and Altair — which by now is sinking into the west. From Deneb, look north for a distinctive five-star pattern resembling a child's drawing of a house, with a square base and pointed roof. That's Cepheus. Its brightest star is Alderamin, about 49 light-years away, which marks one corner of the "house.".

Jamie is an experienced science and travel journalist, stargazer and eclipse chaser who writes about exploring the night sky, solar and lunar eclipses, the Northern Lights, moon-gazing, astro-travel, astronomy and space exploration. He is the editor of WhenIsTheNextEclipse.com, author of A Stargazing Program For Beginners, co-author of The Eclipse Effect, and a senior contributor at Forbes.

A lot goes down in Yellowjackets' Season 4 premiere! The team returns to civilization in the past timeline. Meanwhile, in the present, Misty (Christina Ricci) is plotting to kill Shauna (Melanie Lynskey), while Melissa's (Hilary Swank) looking to outwit the former Antler Queen with a big move.

She races back to camp, shouting, "It worked! We're getting rescued." But as she reaches the team's shelters, she stops in her tracks, and notes, "What the fuck?" as she looks at...something.

The following morning is when Shauna (Sophie Nélisse) realizes Hannah has been wearing Natalie's garb to hide her absence from the ritual.

It has been revealed that so, option one is that Natalie, who ran back to the camp not with joy but determination, was hoping to stop the hunt with the news. But she arrived to find Mari like the frog scientists had found Coach Ben (Steven Krueger): ritualistically slaughtered and cut to pieces.

Option 2 relates to the episode's opening credits. Season after season, Yellowjackets has teased details of future episodes through imagery in the title sequence. In the premiere episode, those images included an image of Teen Shauna lying on her back in the snow, badly beaten.
