#59205. MIT discovers that aging weakens the brain’s nighttime cleaning system

📅 18 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 8m • 📚 Deep Dive (1665 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Sciencedaily ↗ Open Full Page

MIT discovers that aging weakens the brain’s nighttime cleaning system

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1665 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • While we sleep, the brain carries out an essential maintenance process that helps wash away accumulated waste.
  • Industry observers note that researchers discovered that waves of cerebrospinal fluid (CSF), which help carry waste out of the brain, are significantly weaker in older adults.
  • The findings raise important questions about whether weakened brain cleansing could contribute to Alzheimer's disease and other forms of dementia.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

While we sleep, the brain carries out an essential maintenance process that helps wash away accumulated waste. But new research from MIT suggests that this natural cleaning system becomes less effective as we grow older, revealing another way aging can change the brain beyond simply disrupting sleep.

Industry observers note that researchers discovered that waves of cerebrospinal fluid (CSF), which help carry waste out of the brain, are significantly weaker in older adults. The decline appears to be connected to changes in the slow electrical waves that occur during deep sleep, as well as changes in how blood moves through the brain. Importantly, the reduced fluid movement cannot be explained simply by older people spending less time asleep.

The findings raise important questions about whether weakened brain cleansing could contribute to Alzheimer's disease and other forms of dementia. The team now hopes to determine whether changes in these fluid waves could eventually help identify people at greater risk of cognitive decline.

In a recent development, "We know that people age really differently. Some people age very successfully with great cognitive outcomes, and other people develop cognitive decline. If we can figure out who has great trajectories of aging and what are the factors that are associated with that, we might be able to use that to predict future outcomes," notes Laura Lewis, the Athinoula A. Martinos Associate Professor of Electrical Engineering and Computer Science, a member of MIT's Institute for Medical Engineering and Science and the Research Laboratory of Electronics, and an associate member of the Picower Institute for Learning and Memory.

Lewis and her colleagues also want to investigate whether treatments or other interventions could strengthen this waste-clearing process in older adults.

The study was published in Nature Aging, with Lewis serving as senior author. Its lead authors are Sydney Bailes, a postdoctoral researcher in MIT's Laboratory for Information and Decision Systems, and Stephanie Williams, a former MIT visiting student who received her PhD from Boston University in 2026.

How Deep Sleep Helps the Brain Clear Waste.

Deep sleep does much more than leave us feeling refreshed. During its deepest stages, known as non-REM sleep, the brain produces powerful, slow electrical waves that support physical recovery, strengthen memories, and help regulate other essential functions.

In a recent development, in 2019, Lewis and her colleagues discovered that these slow brain waves also help generate rhythmic movements of cerebrospinal fluid. The fluid moves through spaces around the brain and plays an notable role in carrying away waste products.

According to recent reports, that earlier discovery led to a upcoming question. Because slow brain waves typically weaken with age, could the fluid movements responsible for clearing waste also become less effective?

In a recent development, previous research had produced conflicting results. Some studies suggested that cerebrospinal fluid movement declined with age, while others reported increases. However, those investigations had not directly monitored the fluid during sleep, when the brain's natural cleaning activity is especially notable.

Sources indicate that to investigate, the MIT team recruited two groups of volunteers. Younger participants were between 18 and 39 years old, while the older group ranged from 60 to 84.

Each volunteer completed a testing session lasting approximately two hours. The sessions began late at night, increasing the likelihood that participants would become sleepy during the measurements.

According to recent reports, the researchers combined several techniques to observe what was happening inside the brain. Functional magnetic resonance imaging, or fMRI, allowed them to track changes in cerebral blood flow. A specialized MRI method developed by Lewis measured cerebrospinal fluid movement, while electroencephalography, or EEG, recorded the brain's electrical activity.

Many participants fell asleep inside the scanner, providing an opportunity to compare their brain activity and fluid movements during wakefulness and sleep.

The results revealed a striking age difference. As younger adults entered non-REM sleep, their slow brain waves grew stronger and were accompanied by larger waves of cerebrospinal fluid. In older adults, however, the average fluid waves were substantially smaller.

The findings showed that aging was associated with a weakening of the fluid movements that normally accompany deep sleep.

Why the Aging Brain's Cleaning Waves Weaken.

The researchers next investigated what might be causing this decline. In a separate set of experiments conducted while participants were fully awake, they examined how the brain's blood vessels responded to different demands.

One possible explanation involved neurovascular coupling, the process that connects brain activity with blood flow.

When a particular region of the brain becomes more active, its cells require additional oxygen and nutrients. Nearby blood vessels normally widen to deliver more blood, ensuring that the active cells receive the resources they need.

Industry observers note that to measure this response, the researchers showed volunteers a flickering checkerboard pattern while monitoring blood flow with fMRI. The rapidly changing visual pattern stimulates activity in regions involved in processing vision, which should trigger an increase in local blood supply.

In many older participants, the brain's electrical activity increased as expected, but the corresponding rise in blood flow was much smaller. This suggested that aging had weakened the ability of blood vessels to respond to the brain's changing oxygen requirements.

The team then performed a second experiment to examine the brain's broader vascular responsiveness.

Participants were instructed to hold their breath while researchers monitored changes in cerebral blood flow. Holding one's breath causes carbon dioxide to accumulate in the bloodstream, which normally prompts blood vessels in the brain to widen and increase blood flow.

It has been revealed that once again, the older group showed a weaker response. On average, their cerebral blood flow increased less than it did in younger volunteers.

Together, these experiments indicated that changes in the brain's vascular system could help explain why its waste-clearing fluid waves diminish with age.

Using a statistical model, the scientists found that weakened neurovascular coupling and reduced blood flow responses accounted for much of the decline in cerebrospinal fluid movement. However, the two mechanisms did not explain the entire difference, suggesting that additional biological changes associated with aging are also involved.

It has been revealed that "Aging is so complex, and so many different things change, that it's really hard to disentangle the individual factors," Bailes says. "We try to account for some of the mechanisms, but there definitely are a lot of other factors related to vascular health and lifestyle. If you were able to measure all of them, you might be able to break it apart into different explanations for why an individual's CSF flow might be more or less impaired.".

Could Weaker Brain Cleansing Increase Dementia Risk?

The discovery may have important implications for understanding neurological diseases associated with aging.

Sources indicate that earlier studies have linked disrupted sleep to a greater risk of Alzheimer's disease and other forms of dementia. Because cerebrospinal fluid helps remove waste from the brain, researchers are particularly interested in whether age-related changes in its movement might contribute to neurodegeneration.

Sources indicate that none of the volunteers in the MIT study had been diagnosed with a neurodegenerative disorder. However, brain scans revealed that some older participants highlighted signs of gray matter atrophy, meaning a loss of brain tissue in regions containing large numbers of nerve cells.

Those changes were associated with greater reductions in cerebrospinal fluid movement.

The relationship does not establish that weakened fluid flow causes brain tissue loss or dementia. Nevertheless, it provides a reason to investigate whether these changes might serve as early warning signs of neurological decline.

The researchers hope to follow some of the participants over time to determine whether reduced cerebrospinal fluid movement is associated with a greater likelihood of developing a neurodegenerative condition.

Can the Brain's Nighttime Cleaning System Be Restored?

Beyond understanding why brain cleansing declines, the MIT team is exploring whether it might be possible to improve the process.

One promising possibility involves sound stimulation during sleep.

In a separate recent study, Lewis' laboratory found that brief bursts of "pink noise" could increase cerebrospinal fluid movement in younger adults. Pink noise is a type of sound that contains a broad range of frequencies, with greater emphasis on lower frequencies than white noise.

Although the approach has shown potential in younger people, researchers have not yet tested whether it can produce similar effects in older adults.

Another intriguing finding could provide clues about how to preserve the brain's natural cleaning abilities.

Industry observers note that while older participants generally had weaker cerebrospinal fluid waves than younger adults, the decline was not universal. Some older volunteers retained fluid movements that were comparable to those measured in healthy younger people.

This raises the possibility that certain biological or lifestyle factors may help protect the brain's waste-removal system against aging.

"It's really intriguing that for some of these older adults, their CSF fell right in the range of the healthy young adults," Lewis says. "We are really interested in what's different in those people and how that might be related to future health outcomes.".

Understanding why some older brains maintain these youthful fluid movements could ultimately help researchers identify ways to support healthier brain aging and investigate whether preserving the brain's nighttime cleaning system can reduce the risk of cognitive decline.

The research received funding from the National Institutes of Health, the Simons Collaboration on Plasticity in the Aging Brain, a McKnight Scholar Award, a Pew Biomedical Scholar Award, an MIT EECS Transformative Research Award, the Picower Institute Neurological Disorder Discovery Research Fund, a Sloan Fellowship, and the Department of Defense National Defense Science and Engineering Graduate Fellowship Program.

The NO FAKES Act was introduced by Sen. Chris Coons (D-ME) in May, following a previous attempt at the bill last year. While it advanced out of the Senate Judiciary Committee in June and has a bipartisan coalition of co-sponsors, the full Senate has not taken it up. Lourd wrote that the bill would introduce a federal standard for “control, consent and compensation” surrounding deepfakes, replacing “outdated, ill-fitting state laws, many of them written with an analog world in mind.” Related Stories ‘Your Daughter’ Director on Bonds With Mom, Marianne Khoury, and 'Uncle Joe,' Youssef Chahine: ‘Filmmaking Is Really About Healing’ How to Watch 'Yellowjackets’ Season 4 Online: The Hit Thriller Returns for Its Final Season.

“I come to this issue not as a policymaker but as a practitioner. I run a global talent agency. Industry observers note that lourd laid out the stakes for Hollywood by citing Tom Hanks, who warned his followers in 2023 about a dental office using an AI deepfake of a younger version of him in an advertisement. Hanks likely wouldn’t have agreed to the dental ad, Lourd wrote, but he should’ve been given a choice before the dental office ran with an unauthorized deepfake.

CAA has advocated against the unauthorized proliferation of celebrity deepfakes online, working with the Cate Blanchett-backed Human Consent Foundation to help people control permissions for their likenesses if they’re scraped by AI models. Recent findings suggest that deepfakes have been a constant presence since large-language models emerged in 2022, with many being used to produce unauthorized and sometimes explicit depictions of actors, singers and other celebrities. #59201. Uranus and Neptune’s bizarre magnetic fields may finally be explained

Uranus and Neptune’s bizarre magnetic fields may finally be explained

📅 15 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1131 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • When NASA's Voyager 2 spacecraft visited Uranus and Neptune in the 1980s, it discovered something extraordinary.
  • Sources indicate that now, researchers believe they may have found an answer hidden deep inside these enormous worlds.
  • The research, published in Communications Physics, was led by scientists at The University of Texas at Austin in collaboration with researchers from the University of California, Los Angeles, Imperial College London, and Northumbria University.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

When NASA's Voyager 2 spacecraft visited Uranus and Neptune in the 1980s, it discovered something extraordinary. Unlike Earth, which has a relatively orderly magnetic field with clearly defined north and south poles, both distant planets possess strangely distorted and dramatically tilted magnetic fields. For decades, scientists have struggled to explain why.

Sources indicate that now, researchers believe they may have found an answer hidden deep inside these enormous worlds. A new study suggests that changes in how well materials conduct electricity under extreme conditions could explain the planets' unusual magnetism. The findings also raise an intriguing possibility: the magnetic fields of Uranus and Neptune may change dramatically over just a few decades.

The research, published in Communications Physics, was led by scientists at The University of Texas at Austin in collaboration with researchers from the University of California, Los Angeles, Imperial College London, and Northumbria University.

Why Uranus and Neptune Have Such Strange Magnetic Fields.

Recent findings suggest that planetary magnetic fields originate deep beneath the surface, where moving fluids capable of conducting electricity generate magnetic forces. Scientists call this process a dynamo.

Industry observers note that on Earth, the dynamo operates within the outer core, a layer of molten metal surrounded by mostly solid rock. As liquid iron circulates and the planet rotates, it generates a magnetic field resembling that of a giant bar magnet. This produces the familiar north and south magnetic poles that allow compasses to point in a consistent direction.

Recent findings suggest that earth's magnetic field is also closely aligned with its rotation axis. Its main magnetic axis, known as a dipole, is tilted by only 11 degrees. Uranus and Neptune are strikingly different. Uranus has a magnetic dipole tilted by 59 degrees, while Neptune's is tilted by 47 degrees.

Explaining these extreme tilts requires a better understanding of what lies inside the two planets.

Uranus and Neptune are classified as ice giants, a name that reflects their presumed composition rather than suggesting they are simply frozen worlds. Each is approximately four times wider than Earth, and scientists believe their interiors contain substantial amounts of hydrogen, helium, water, ammonia, methane, and rocky material. However, their precise internal compositions remain uncertain.

Extreme Conditions Deep Inside the Ice Giants.

Chi Yan, the study's lead author and a research associate at the UT Jackson School of Geosciences, believes the combination of the planets' enormous size and unusual chemical makeup may help explain their distorted magnetic fields.

According to recent reports, "Deep inside Uranus and Neptune, pressures and temperatures become extremely high," said Yan. "Under these conditions, which can cause water molecules to break apart into ions, the material may become increasingly electrically conductive with depth.".

Recent findings suggest that ions are electrically charged particles that can carry electric current. If the materials inside Uranus and Neptune become more conductive at greater depths, that could significantly influence how their magnetic fields are generated.

To investigate this possibility, the researchers developed computer simulations designed to reproduce the strange magnetic fields recorded by Voyager 2.

Industry observers note that their models assumed that electrical conductivity increases deeper inside the planets. The researchers also tested a variety of possible internal structures, examining how circulating fluids, temperature changes, and magnetic forces interact over time.

The results suggest that these changing electrical properties could play a crucial role in producing the unusual magnetic fields observed around both ice giants.

Magnetic Poles Could Shift Dramatically Within Decades.

Perhaps the most surprising finding is that the magnetic fields of Uranus and Neptune may be far less stable than Earth's.

Sources indicate that according to the simulations, their magnetic axes could undergo substantial changes in relatively short periods. In some scenarios, the magnetic tilt shifted by tens of degrees within only a few decades.

That raises the possibility that the magnetic fields surrounding Uranus and Neptune today are significantly different from those measured when Voyager 2 flew past them in the 1980s.

Industry observers note that "Earth's magnetic tilt drifts by only a degree or so over 50 years," mentioned Yan. "Our models show the ice giants can behave very differently. In some stretches the tilt swings by tens of degrees within decades. In others it shifts only slightly over the same span.".

These dramatic changes remain predictions from computer models rather than confirmed observations. However, scientists may already have a way to look for evidence of them.

James Webb Telescope Could Reveal Magnetic Changes.

Sources indicate that researchers are now examining detailed infrared images of Uranus and Neptune captured by the James Webb Space Telescope (JWST). They are particularly interested in the planets' auroras, which form when charged particles from the Sun interact with gases in their atmospheres.

According to recent reports, auroras are closely connected to planetary magnetic fields, making them valuable clues to what is happening far above the planets' hidden interiors. Changes in the appearance and arrangement of these glowing atmospheric features could help researchers determine whether the magnetic poles have shifted since Voyager 2's encounters.

"We are busy working on what's contained within these observations, but the shape and structure of the aurora, as well as other weird patterns in the ionosphere, promises to provide us with a way of understanding how the magnetic fields have changed, an notable stepping stone," stated Tom Stallard, a professor at Northumbria University who led the JWST observation campaign and reviewed the paper for the journal.

It has been revealed that the ionosphere is a region of the upper atmosphere containing electrically charged particles. Its behavior is influenced by magnetic activity, offering another potential source of information about the planets' changing magnetic environments.

The research team hopes to combine Webb's auroral observations with Voyager 2's original magnetic field measurements and the new dynamo simulations. Together, these sources of evidence could provide the clearest picture yet of how the magnetic fields of Uranus and Neptune are arranged today.

In a recent development, even so, scientists emphasize that fully understanding the planets' deep interiors will require upcoming spacecraft missions to these distant worlds. Until then, improved simulations and powerful telescopes may help unravel one of the solar system's most unusual magnetic mysteries.

The research was funded by The University of Texas Institute for Geophysics (UTIG) in the Jackson School of Geosciences, the National Aeronautics and Space Administration (NASA), and the Science and Technology Facilities Council.

Trouble at Mars: NASA's Perseverance rover, Odyssey orbiter halt science work due to glitches

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (995 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Space

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Two of NASA's Mars explorers are sidelined by glitches at the moment.
  • Industry observers note that the Perseverance rover and Mars Odyssey orbiter have stood down from science work due to technical problems, NASA revealed on Thursday (Nov.
  • Recent findings suggest that perseverance has been sidelined by an antenna matter, and the venerable Odyssey is dealing with a balky reaction wheel.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Two of NASA's Mars explorers are sidelined by glitches at the moment.

Industry observers note that the Perseverance rover and Mars Odyssey orbiter have stood down from science work due to technical problems, NASA revealed on Thursday (Nov. 19).

Recent findings suggest that perseverance has been sidelined by an antenna matter, and the venerable Odyssey is dealing with a balky reaction wheel. NASA hopes both can get back to work at Mars by the end of November.

Perseverance landed inside Mars' Jezero Crater in February 2021, tasked with assessing the area's potential to support past life and with collecting dozens of samples for future return to Earth.

It has done all this and more. The Perseverance team has determined that Jezero hosted a potentially habitable lake billions of years ago. And the car-sized rover has found a wealth of complex organic compounds in Martian rock, some of which might themselves be signs of life (though assessing this hypothesis fully will likely require bringing Perseverance's samples to Earth for analysis, scientists stress).

In addition, Perseverance just set a upcoming distance record for off-Earth driving, rolling past the mark set by its smaller cousin, NASA's Opportunity rover (28.06 miles, or 45.16 kilometers).

Perseverance broke that record on Oct. 11. Just 19 days later, however, the mission team noticed a problem: The rover's main UHF downlink radio — which it uses to send information home to Earth, via data-relay satellites in Mars orbit — failed to send its usual "heartbeat" pings to the main computer.

Perseverance detected this problem autonomously and reacted as it was programmed to do: The six-wheeled robot switched to its backup UHF radio and went into a protective "safe mode," shutting down all non-essential systems.

The rover team recovered Perseverance from safe mode but soon noticed another issue: "The backup UHF radio was transmitting at about half of its expected power output," NASA officials wrote in an patch on Thursday.

Perseverance's handlers have stopped using that backup radio as well; the rover is now communicating with Earth directly (without the help of relay orbiters), sending signals to NASA's Deep Space Network dishes via its high-gain antenna.

Recent findings suggest that this pathway features lower data rates, and the mission team wants to prioritize the delivery of diagnostic information. So they've paused Perseverance's science work, which includes observations by its various cameras.

The glitch may be disappointing to devoted Perseverance fans, many of whom have already noticed that the mission website hasn't uploaded any latest raw images since Nov. 7. But there's no reason to panic, according to NASA.

In a recent development, "The rover is stable and communicating with the team," agency officials wrote in Thursday's revision. "The team is hopeful the rover could return to science by the end of November, and NASA will provide further updates in the future as the team works the issue.".

Mars Odyssey's problem may be more serious: The orbiter, which arrived at the Red Planet in October 2001, recently lost the use of one of its reaction wheels.

Odyssey has four reaction wheels, which help the spacecraft maintain its orientation in space. Three of the four must be functional to do this job, and Odyssey already lost a reaction wheel in 2013.

This latest issue cropped up on Nov. 4, when Odyssey went into safe mode. The orbiter stayed in this protective posture until Nov. 6 while mission team members diagnosed and dealt with the problem. They've made some progress, at one point getting the faulty wheel to move when commanded.

"Further testing is being conducted to confirm whether the wheel is recoverable," NASA officials wrote in Thursday's revision.

Sources indicate that though it has been out of safe mode for two weeks, Odyssey still has not resumed its science or data-relay work. (The orbiter has long helped NASA's Mars surface craft send information home to Earth.).

"The goal is for Odyssey to return to science and relay operations at the conclusion of these tests and analysis during the last week of November, and NASA will provide future updates on status and timeline as the team learns more," agency officials wrote in the revision.

If the reaction wheel, isn't recoverable, Odyssey's days are numbered. The mission team will have to orient the orbiter solely using its thrusters, and Odyssey has enough hydrazine fuel left to do this for a just month or two, according to NASA.

Odyssey's mission has been a rousing success, no matter what happens with the reaction wheel. The orbiter has operated at Mars longer than any other spacecraft, and it has made a number of crucial scientific contributions.

"Odyssey created the first global maps detailing the composition of the Martian surface, which have become foundational for Mars geologists," NASA officials wrote in Thursday's patch.

"The orbiter's surface maps have also played a key role in identifying hazards at landing sites, spotting locations of scientific interest for landers and rovers to explore, and mapping water molecules in the top 3 feet (1 meter) of the surface, including buried ice that could be useful to the first astronauts on Mars.".

Let's kick things off with the Season 4 premiere:.

Sample lyric: If I could find that Heina / And that Sancho that she's found / Well, I'd pop a cap in Sancho / And I'd slap her down.

Season 4 opens with this hit song that had a total chokehold on teens in 1996. The lyrics sing of a hapless dude making messy decisions.

In a recent development, fittingly, it plays while teen Jeff (Jack DePew) is getting high on the job at Taylor's Furniture Store with his doofy bestie Randy (Riley Baron). Despite some violent lyrics, "Santeria" is a upbeat tune that speaks to Jeff's laid-back attitude, post-graduation.

But once he sees the news of the Yellowjackets rescue on TV, the theme song cuts in and dramatically changes the episode's tone.

Sample lyric: It was cool / Nothing fire / Nothing broke / Keep simple / Nothing tired / Nothing old / Same as you / Same as you.

For four seasons now, this song's cryptic lyrics have played as a pitch-perfect distillation of the show's female rage, rooted in lust, jealousy, and even love.

Sample lyric: My girl, my girl, don't lie to me / Tell me, where did you sleep last night?In the pines, in the pines / Where the sun don't ever shine / I would shiver the whole night through.

After the opening credits, Yellowjackets picks up with the titular team in a hospital, where they are safe but look worried, likely about the world learning how it is they made it through their ordeal.

Playing over the sequence is Kurt Cobain's cover of the American folk song also known as "In the Pines," which is recognized as a murder ballad. The lyrics reflect a haunting story of homicide in the woods. The particular song has been covered by a variety of acts since its creation in the 1870s, including the father of Bluegrass Bill Monroe, Blues singer Lead Belly, and Dolly Parton.

Industry observers note that cobain famously covered the song on his MTV Unplugged appearance, on Nov. 18, 1993. So, it's a cover the Yellowjackets themselves might recognize. Moreover, his grunge rendition reflects the trauma and terror of the team's return to civilization.

Sample lyric: For the life of me, I cannot remember / What made us think that we were wise and we'd never compromise / For the life of me, I cannot believe / We'd ever die for these sins, we were merely freshmen.

This '90s song plays in the present timeline, but in a meaningful way. Showing up to Shauna's (Melanie Lynskey) door in episode 1, Melissa (Hilary Swank) presents a bottle of wine along with the news that she's moved in next door, and that she's called the press. Shauna looks on in shock asking, "What did you do?" as "The Freshmen" plays.

From 1997, this hit song from the Verve Pipe tells the tale of two young men, reflecting on the damage they've done to a shared lover. In this context, "The Freshmen" plays as if Shauna's subconscious is making an excuse ("we were merely freshmen").

Or perhaps, this song's use use here is meant to reflect Melissa's perspective. As the wounded lover, her story could show what might happen if that lover struck back with the poetic justice of reclaiming her narrative and her future.

#59197. Rejecting cheap fabrics, higher prices: Why shoppers are asking for better clothes

📅 20 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1272 w)

General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 CNBC ↗ Open Full Page

Rejecting cheap fabrics, higher prices: Why shoppers are asking for better clothes

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1272 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: CNBC

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Clothing isn't made like it used to be, and more shoppers are taking notice.
  • The makeup of apparel imported into the U.S.
  • In a recent development, apparel prices generally declined over the two decades leading up to the pandemic, according to the consumer price index.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Clothing isn't made like it used to be, and more shoppers are taking notice.

The makeup of apparel imported into the U.S. has shifted in recent years. In 2010, about 60% of clothing was predominantly made from cotton. Now, that total is around 45%, while predominantly synthetic fabrics such as polyester and nylon comprise the majority of imports.

In a recent development, apparel prices generally declined over the two decades leading up to the pandemic, according to the consumer price index. Since 2020, they have soared to record highs.

It's starting to change habits for consumers who are paying more for food, gas, rent and other staples. As shoppers shell out more for clothes, they're increasingly making sure the garments are worth the cost.

Consulting firm AlixPartners' 2026 Consumer Sentiment Index, which surveyed more than 9,000 shoppers, found that consumers are scrutinizing labels more closely and rejecting cheap materials sold at a premium.

"If it's not a natural material, a retailer brand who passes it off as it is, they're really becoming very low on consumers' minds," remarked Sonia Lapinsky, head of fashion at AlixPartners.

Industry observers note that fast fashion brands like Forever 21 and H&M exploded in popularity during the early 2000s and 2010s, bringing trendy clothing to shelves quickly at low prices. Then came ultra-fast fashion, with brands like Shein and Fashion Nova pumping out latest garments at even quicker speeds and lower price points — made possible in part through the use of inexpensive, synthetic fabrics.

"We got to a point where the pendulum just swung too far in that direction. And we've actually begun to see a reversal," stated U.S. Bancorp BTIG consumer analyst Janine Stichter. "Quality matters a lot more ... over the last three or four years than it has in the previous 10 or 20.".

But quality, which shoppers often tie directly to material, can come at a higher cost.

According to recent reports, the average unit price of apparel imported to the U.S. between January and August was $2.64 per square meter for garments that were predominantly synthetic fiber, like polyester and nylon, compared with $3.67 for items that were largely cotton, according to data from the U.S. Commerce Department's Office of Textiles and Apparel.

When comparing those 2026 figures to 2010, synthetic fiber apparel import costs have climbed around 11%, while cotton apparel costs have risen 21%.

"If you're appealing to a more value-sensitive customer, you either reduce the quality, or you negotiate with suppliers to try to share some of the cost or you maybe absorb the cost … and perhaps hope to crank a higher volume of product to make up for it," said Bernstein Research senior retail analyst Aneesha Sherman.

Recent findings suggest that though polyester is cheaper, experts point out that's not necessarily a bad thing. It can help clothing hold its shape and wick away sweat.

Sherman believes the athleisure boom is a primary factor in the shift toward polyester. She said that from 2015 to 2025, sports apparel was growing at a 4.9% rate in the U.S., versus 2.6% for all apparel and footwear, according to Euromonitor data.

"There probably is some quality trade down as well happening there," Sherman said. "But I think both these trends are conflated.".

Nonetheless, backlash to synthetic materials is growing. Gen Z has even repurposed the word "polyester" as an insult to mean generally low-quality or fake.

Concerns have also grown about the environment and human health surrounding petroleum-based clothing, as more research indicates microplastics can leach from polyester clothing when washed.

It's led consumers to reexamine what materials are in their clothing.

Apparel prices have risen coming out of the pandemic, as demand outpaced supply and allowed companies to raise prices, mentioned BTIG's Stichter. Tariffs and the Iran war followed, raising costs for businesses — and prices for consumers.

Petroleum is the basis of many synthetic fibers, and oil prices have skyrocketed since the start of the Iran war.

The same factors that helped drive up prices of clothing — Covid, tariffs and war — also affected clothing quality.

"Companies had to move around their supply chains in the post-Covid period," mentioned Stichter. "They had to find ways to take costs out, and sometimes that meant using less expensive fabrics.".

Those factors compounded a more-than-decade-long shift away from manufacturing in China.

Sheng Lu, a fashion and apparel studies professor at the University of Delaware, whose research focuses on the economics of the global textile industry, said China's established history with clothing production means it has higher-skilled workers, state-of-the-art-equipment and better material management compared with emerging manufacturing destinations such as Bangladesh, Sri Lanka and Cambodia.

Sources indicate that "They mostly serve the value market and the mass market. And I think the reason why they're not ready to make higher-quality luxury and premium products really reflects the kind of skill sets you can expect when you source from these countries," mentioned Lu.

AlixPartners' Lapinsky said these countries that manufacture at a lower cost sometimes have to still ship the raw materials from China, which can extend the timeline to make clothing. That means taking earlier bets on trends and then discounting if products don't sell well.

"If you have to mark down that product because the consumer doesn't want it as much, your net margin might actually be worse than if you were to just invest in quality in the first place," remarked BTIG's Stichter.

And as material costs rise for synthetic fibers, Stichter also mentioned she believes it could further influence companies to use more natural fabrics moving forward.

Companies prioritizing quality are winning in this environment.

Ralph Lauren's stock is up around 85% over the past two years. Around 90% of its apparel is primarily made of cotton, leather, wool, viscose, cashmere or silk, according to its 2026 sustainability report. In its fiscal 2026, the company said it sold more products at full price and reduced markdowns.

Meanwhile, direct-to-consumer clothing brand Quince, which centers its brand identity around natural materials, reached a $10 billion valuation this year.

The brand jumped 16 spots to No. 3 for best resale value in online consignment retailer ThredUp's 2025 report. Organic cotton retailer Pact jumped 20 spots on that list to No. 8, illustrating the potential role materials are playing in brand recognition.

Alternatively, the 2026 AlixPartners report, which ranks sentiment for brands in different retail categories, found shoppers are viewing some fast fashion brands less favorably. Both Shein and Zara dropped three spots — to fifth and seventh place, respectively — in terms of sentiment in the young adult specialty category.

Shein passed higher tariff costs onto shoppers in 2025 and then blamed a sales slowdown on those higher prices. The ultra-fast fashion retailer saw its year-over-year share of U.S. apparel, accessories and footwear card spending decrease in the fourth quarter of 2025 and first two quarters of 2026, according to Consumer Edge.

Shein did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

It has been revealed that though Zara fell in AlixPartners' Consumer Sentiment Index, it has continued to grow sales and profits year over year. Even so, Lapinsky said worsening consumer views are something to watch, even if the organization is doing well.

"What we found over the years with this consumer sentiment index is that sometimes it will be a bit of a leading indicator of what's to come," said AlixPartners' Lapinsky. "I'm not saying that this is going to be true for Zara, but I think that's one thing that we'll be watching as we look in the upcoming quarters and into 2027.".

An ancient virus may help explain what makes the human brain different

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (964 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, A virus that infected chimpanzees millions of years ago has left behind a genetic legacy that may help explain an important difference between human and chimpanzee brain development.
  • The findings, published in Science Advances, reveal how infections from the distant past can leave lasting changes in the genetic makeup of an entire population.
  • In a recent development, although pandemics are often considered a modern threat, infectious diseases have been spreading through large animal and human populations for millions of years.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, A virus that infected chimpanzees millions of years ago has left behind a genetic legacy that may help explain an important difference between human and chimpanzee brain development. Researchers at Lund University have discovered that ancient viral DNA embedded in the chimpanzee genome switches off a gene that remains active in humans and appears to play an important role in the developing brain.

The findings, published in Science Advances, reveal how infections from the distant past can leave lasting changes in the genetic makeup of an entire population. They also offer new clues about how the brains of humans and our closest evolutionary relatives may have developed differently.

In a recent development, although pandemics are often considered a modern threat, infectious diseases have been spreading through large animal and human populations for millions of years. Some of these ancient infections left traces of viral DNA that continue to influence how genes function today.

Johan Jakobsson, Professor of Molecular Neurogenetics at Lund University, states the discovery demonstrates how a virus can introduce genetic changes that eventually become widespread throughout a population.

Sources indicate that "The virus we investigated specifically affected chimpanzees. Yet humans and chimpanzees have largely the same genetic makeup. That is why it is key to understand the differences in how genes are regulated. Our findings suggest that one gene, LINC00662, plays a significant role in early human brain development," states Johan Jakobsson.

How an Ancient Virus Silenced a Brain Development Gene.

According to recent reports, at the center of the discovery is a gene called LINC00662. Researchers found that it is active during early human brain development but completely switched off in comparable chimpanzee brain models.

In a recent development, the difference appears to be caused by a genetic remnant of PTERV1, an ancient virus that infected chimpanzees millions of years ago. PTERV1 belongs to a group known as endogenous retroviruses, which are viruses whose genetic material became incorporated into the DNA of their hosts. Once embedded in the genome, these viral sequences can be inherited by future generations.

Over time, PTERV1 produced numerous copies of its genetic material that became scattered across different parts of the chimpanzee genome. Researchers found that these viral sequences are systematically silenced through a process called methylation.

Methylation involves chemical modifications to DNA that help regulate gene activity. It is one of the ways cells control which genetic instructions are used and which remain inactive. In this case, the ancient viral insertion appears to have caused a neighboring gene involved in brain development to be switched off.

Jakobsson indicates understanding these differences in gene regulation could also provide vital insights into how genetic activity protects the brain or contributes to damage and disease.

Miniature Brains Reveal a Striking Genetic Difference.

To investigate the virus's effects, researchers grew miniature brain models called organoids using stem cells from humans and chimpanzees. These three-dimensional structures reproduce certain features of developing brain tissue, allowing scientists to study aspects of early brain development under controlled laboratory conditions.

According to recent reports, when the team compared the two types of organoids, the difference was striking. LINC00662 showed strong activity in the human brain models but was completely inactive in those derived from chimpanzee cells.

"The gene was strongly expressed in the human organoids, but not at all in the chimpanzee organoids," says Patricia Gerdes, postdoc in molecular neurogenetics at Lund University.

The researchers then set out to determine whether the ancient viral DNA was directly responsible for this difference.

Using CRISPR-Cas9, a powerful gene editing technology that allows scientists to make targeted changes to DNA, they removed the viral sequence from chimpanzee cells.

The result provided compelling evidence. Once the viral DNA was removed, the previously inactive LINC00662 gene switched back on.

"This shows that it is in fact the viral insertion that is responsible for the gene being switched off in chimpanzees," says Patricia Gerdes.

New Clues to Human Brain Evolution.

It has been revealed that the team also wanted to understand what LINC00662 actually does in the human brain. To investigate, they used CRISPR to switch off the gene in human brain organoids and examined how other genes responded.

Sources indicate that disabling LINC00662 reduced the activity of genes associated with nerve cell development and the formation of connections between neurons. These processes are essential for establishing the networks that allow the brain to communicate and function.

The results suggest that LINC00662 contributes to important stages of early human brain development, while the ancient viral insertion prevents the gene from functioning in chimpanzees.

Recent findings suggest that more broadly, the discovery highlights an crucial principle of evolution. Although humans and chimpanzees share much of their genetic material, differences in how genes are switched on and off can influence how their bodies and brains develop.

The findings suggest that ancient viral infections may have contributed to these differences by altering gene regulation long after the original infections disappeared.

Researchers now strategy to investigate whether other remnants of ancient viruses have similarly influenced brain evolution. They also hope to determine whether these inherited viral sequences may play a role in neurological diseases.

Together, the discoveries raise an intriguing possibility that some of the differences between human and chimpanzee brains may trace back, at least in part, to viruses that infected our evolutionary relatives millions of years ago.

#59194. Don’t Bring Jensen Back

📅 20 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1315 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 WIRED ↗ Open Full Page

Don’t Bring Jensen Back

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1315 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: WIRED

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that early in Shakespeare’s tragedy Julius Caesar, the title character is publicly offered a crown as a symbol of absolute power.
  • He did not even wait until a crown was offered before grabbing for it.
  • Huang, used to exercising power, seemed as energized as the mob supporting Caesar had been.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that early in Shakespeare’s tragedy Julius Caesar, the title character is publicly offered a crown as a symbol of absolute power. Caesar refuses it three times, dramatically fainting after the final try. Scholars say that Caesar’s “falling sickness,” as his eventual assassin Brutus put it, masked his true intention to rule. His effort to win over the crowd with his humility only intensified the momentum to grant him more power. Indeed, after his refusal, his adherents became even more impassioned, setting the stage for his eventual claim to kingship. “If Caesar had stabb’d their mothers, they would have done no less,” said a Roman senator of the sycophantic crowd.

Jensen Huang was not so strategic. He did not even wait until a crown was offered before grabbing for it. On November 12, Nvidia’s cofounder had resigned from his post as CEO, promising to work to heal his family and earn back trust. The reasons were obvious. He had been engaging in an affair with an alleged Chinese spy. Under his leadership, billions of dollars’ worth of Nvidia’s sales had gone to her formerly obscure company in Singapore, which, in a potential violation of export regulations, the company used to power Chinese AI efforts. In addition, he was carrying on an affair with an Nvidia subordinate (or was it two?), itself a fireable transgression. Nonetheless, because of his success in building Nvidia, Huang has been receiving a noisy groundswell of support from Silicon Valley and Wall Street, with the same loyalty as the crowd that would have idolized Caesar even if he’d stabbed their mothers.

Huang, used to exercising power, seemed as energized as the mob supporting Caesar had been. Social media was exploding with memes portraying him as a hero whose return would result in Homeric redemption. Silicon Valley leaders like Travis Kalanick, Tim Sweeney, and Elon Musk called his removal an injustice that must be addressed. One of Huang’s talents is moving fast. So perhaps he used state-of-the-art Rubin GPUs to dispatch an armada of AI introspection-bots, fast-tracking what formerly would have taken months of moral cleansing into a few days. In any case, on November 17, when the pixels on his resignation message had barely settled, he returned to X to announce that he would be honored to reclaim his position if offered.

It was not to be. Within hours, Nvidia’s board threw more water on Huang’s overture than a Texas data center consumes in a year. During a scheduled earnings call, chair Harvey Jones noted, “The Nvidia board unanimously accepted his resignation but does not intend to reinstate Jensen Huang as CEO.” Nvidia’s interim leader, Colette Kress, who had been its long-time CFO, ended the call with a devastating kicker: “We’ve got this.” Et tu, Colette?

According to recent reports, the search for a replacement will proceed. But even after the board presumably closed the door, and Kress told employees in an all-hands meeting once again that “we got this,” the push to restore him has not quieted. The president of the United States hasn’t retracted his opinion that Huang should resume his post. A petition called “Stand With Jensen” now has over 200,000 signatures. Hedge funder Bill Ackman zinged out a hysterical X post this week charging “major governance failures by directors.” (Clearly, Ackman’s view of ideal governance is no governance.) Most alarmingly, Semafor has reported that Huang himself had spoken to at least one board member about his reinstatement and that several directors may still be open to the possibility. At press time, Huang has not given any public indication that he is no longer angling for a triumphant return.

At the Upcoming York Times DealBook conference, held a day after the earnings call, the Jensen affair dominated the discussion, even as Anthropic was readying the biggest IPO in history. On stage, OpenAI’s Sam Altman and Greg Brockman expressed admiration for Huang but did not recommend his reinstatement. But Anduril CEO Palmer Luckey remarked that “nobody can take Jensen’s place in this critical juncture” because “his personal relations are the reason everyone is willing to do business” with Nvidia. Elon Musk reaffirmed his outrage that Huang had been forced out, saying it was like the Chicago Bulls firing Michael Jordan in his prime during a playoff hot streak. In my informal conversations during breaks, I found people on both sides of the divide. One person was a substantial Nvidia investor who showed me pictures of themselves with Huang. Like many with a financial stake in the tech giant, this individual was eager to see Huang back in charge.

According to recent reports, everyone is in agreement that the Huang story is tragic. But the outcry for Huang’s reinstatement is a broader tragedy, revealing how greed has eclipsed ethics and patriotism. Those clamoring for reinstatement have one argument: that Huang’s leadership was so singular and superlative that he must keep his job. Not doing so would dishonor his previous efforts and degrade Nvidia’s future performance. Essentially, it’s an ends-justify-the-means rationale incompatible with corporate oversight and even fidelity to law and national security.

The push to reinstate Huang is also a grotesque extension of the cult of the founder, which assumes that those who built a firm have unique abilities to run it and should be unconstrained in how they do so. (Serious question: If founders are so great, why do the vast majority of startups fail?).

There’s no question that Huang has built one of the greatest companies ever and delivered historic returns to shareholders. But one irony of the Bring Back Jensen Movement is that this crisis has exposed him, in some respects, as an erratic, even a lousy, CEO. His personal indiscretions cost shareholders almost a trillion dollars! He lied to his board. He pursued a strategy that seems to have violated the spirit if not the law of export regulations. He gave senior executive posts to family members who pursued a passion in the chip business later in life, including his daughter (trained as a chef), son (went to art school and owned a cocktail lounge), and son-in-law (former professional skier). In a public organization, nepotism comes at shareholders’ expense.

On top of that, he failed in a critical duty of a CEO—preparing a succession blueprint. Nvidia has none, solely because Huang acted as if he would run it forever. At DealBook, Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella, after the obligatory expressions of empathy toward Huang, threw some shade on leaders who don’t plan for their departure: “People get old and die,” he stated. “If a firm will succeed, it needs someone to take over. I’ve never trusted a leader, founder or otherwise, who says the institution after I left was completely gone. Like, then what did you build?”.

Finally, if Huang were so passionate about Nvidia’s future, why is he still angling for a return? The possibility, even a remote one, that he will be reinstated may discourage the best candidates from considering an offer to lead Nvidia. If the bubble does pop, Huang will avoid being the face of AI when the fall comes. Remember, things didn’t work out too well for Julius Caesar.

Physicists defy expectations by controlling the magnetic heart of a single atom

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (968 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that researchers at Delft University of Technology (The Netherlands) have accomplished something that physicists previously thought should not be possible.
  • According to recent reports, the findings, published in Nature Communications, also present scientists with a new puzzle.
  • Atoms in magnetic metals such as iron and nickel behave like tiny magnets.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that researchers at Delft University of Technology (The Netherlands) have accomplished something that physicists previously thought should not be possible. Using radio waves, they managed to directly control the magnetic spin of the nucleus inside a single atom. The unexpected result challenges existing assumptions about how atomic magnetism behaves and could eventually lead to fresh ways of storing and retrieving quantum information.

According to recent reports, the findings, published in Nature Communications, also present scientists with a new puzzle. Although the experiment demonstrated that this remarkable level of control is possible, researchers do not yet fully understand the mechanism that makes it work.

The Hidden Magnetism Inside Every Atom.

Atoms in magnetic metals such as iron and nickel behave like tiny magnets. However, the magnetism within an atom comes from different sources. Both electrons and, in some cases, the atomic nucleus possess a quantum property called spin, which can be thought of as a miniature magnetic compass needle.

Recent findings suggest that "By far the strongest magnetism comes from the electrons," says lead researcher Sander Otte. "But in some atoms, the nucleus also carries a spin. That spin is much weaker, but it is also much better shielded from the outside world.".

According to recent reports, that protection makes nuclear spin especially interesting to quantum researchers. Because it is less exposed to disturbances from its surroundings, it could offer a promising way to preserve delicate quantum information.

In a recent development, to investigate these tiny magnetic properties, Otte's team uses a specially modified scanning tunneling microscope. This powerful instrument allows the researchers to deliver electrical signals to individual atoms with extraordinary precision.

Until recently, their experiments concentrated primarily on electron spin because it is easier to detect and measure. The nucleus's magnetic spin could only be observed indirectly through a phenomenon known as the hyperfine interaction, which creates a subtle quantum connection between the spins of the electron and nucleus. This connection can cause the two spins to become slightly entangled, meaning their quantum states are linked.

An Atomic Experiment Produces an Unexpected Result.

It has been revealed that in the latest study, lead author Hester Vennema and her colleagues took a different approach. They simultaneously applied two separate signals to a single atom, with one directed at the electron and the other at the nucleus.

By using these signals together, the researchers could investigate their effects independently. What happened next caught them by surprise.

Recent findings suggest that even when the electron and nuclear spins were largely disentangled, the team was still able to flip the orientation of the nucleus's magnetic spin. Based on their previous understanding, the nucleus should not have responded in this way.

Recent findings suggest that "According to our simple understanding, this should not really happen," says Otte. "The nuclear spin should not be sensitive at all to the electrical signals from a scanning tunneling microscope.".

The result suggests that the interaction between electrical signals and nuclear spin involves a mechanism that scientists have yet to fully explain.

Controlling Quantum Spins Like Guitar Strings.

It has been revealed that achieving this level of precision required the researchers to adapt a technique called double magnetic resonance so it could operate on a single atom. The method allowed them to manipulate the magnetic behavior of the atomic nucleus separately from that of an electron.

Magnetic resonance works by applying a wave signal at a carefully selected frequency to change the orientation of a magnetic spin. However, quantum mechanics restricts these changes to specific allowed transitions, meaning the frequency must be precisely matched to the spin being targeted.

Vennema compares the process to playing a musical instrument.

"You can compare it to the strings of a guitar," Vennema explains. "Each possible spin rotation is like a string with its own note. You have to play precisely the right note to make a particular string vibrate. The "notes" of a nuclear spin are a hundred to a thousand times lower than those of an electron spin.".

Sources indicate that in other words, electrons and atomic nuclei respond to very different frequencies, much as different guitar strings produce different musical notes. By tuning their signals to the appropriate frequencies, the scientists could address the two types of spin separately.

A Quantum Breakthrough With a Mystery Still to Solve.

The discovery could have important implications for the future of quantum information technology. Unlike conventional computers, which store information as bits representing either 0 or 1, quantum systems can use quantum states to encode information in more complex ways.

One major challenge is keeping those states stable long enough for information to be stored and retrieved reliably. Nuclear spins are attractive candidates for quantum memory because they are relatively well isolated from environmental interference.

It has been revealed that the ability to control these spins directly could therefore open fresh possibilities for writing, storing, and reading quantum information. However, the findings represent an early experimental advance rather than a ready-to-use quantum memory technology.

For now, one of the most notable outcomes is the new scientific mystery the experiment has revealed. The researchers have demonstrated an unexpected way to manipulate nuclear spin, but the physical mechanism responsible remains unclear.

"Back to the drawing board, then," states Otte. "That is really how science works. There is always something newly introduced left to figure out.".

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Actors have become increasingly vocal in recent months about their struggles amid the slowdown in production of film and television shows, drawing attention to performers’ hardships in qualifying for their union health plan and even paying their dues.

Facing pressure and online criticism to do something more for floundering members, on Friday the actors’ union SAG-AFTRA announced that its national board had voted unanimously to create a public policy-focused task force to advocate for universal healthcare. The group’s new President’s Healthcare Task Force will “mobilize SAG-AFTRA’s collective strength, public influence, and institutional capacity to advance universal access to affordable, comprehensive, and reliable health care,” the union stated.

According to union president Sean Astin, the SAG-AFTRA Health Plan is on strong financial footing but “a subsantial majority of our members do not qualify” by either not earning the requisite minimum of $28,090 or working 108 applicable days per year.

In a recent development, “This Taskforce seeks a upcoming level of participation in the national movement to expand care for everyone,” Astin added. “We will actively engage with policymakers, gather allies and provide a structured way for our members to participate formally in the process. The President’s Healthcare Taskforce will be an instrument of support in the movement for universal healthcare. The President’s Healthcare Taskforce will be an instrument of support in the movement for universal healthcare.”.

It’s a step, though far from a quick-fix solution to the problems that members have grown louder about in recent weeks. In late October, American Horror Story and Glee actor Cheyenne Jackson introduced the “One Job Away” campaign to draw attention to actors in need of one or a few more jobs to qualify for health insurance. “This is systematic. This is like across the whole swath of SAG actors working right now,” he told The Hollywood Reporter at the time.

According to the latest terms the union negotiated with studios and streamers earlier this year, aimed at addressing healthcare inflation, eligibility premiums and the earnings threshold for health insurance will rise slightly in 2027, with more increases coming in the years after.

Sources indicate that some members have also recently faulted the labor group for dropping its COVID-era policy of keeping performers who were behind on their dues in the union. As of Nov. 1, SAG-AFTRA returned to terminating the memberships of actors who owed dues and, according to Variety, thousands have been dropped from the labor group as a result.

As these concerns were developing, its national board extended union staff leader Duncan Crabtree-Ireland’s contract until 2032 on Oct. 24 and reportedly gave him a 15 percent raise, drawing some further scrutiny. Prior to the reported raise, Crabtree-Ireland, whose title has been expanded to deem him the chief executive officer of the union, was already the highest-paid labor leader in Hollywood with a published gross salary of $1,068,535. The union explained at the time, “The extended term provides for added stability and continuity for the union during a time of unprecedented industry disruption.” But some members found the timing insensitive.

Industry observers note that once seen as a progressive pipe dream, universal healthcare may be becoming more politically palatable after a midterm election that hinged on affordability concerns and amid rampant healthcare inflation. But achieving it would, to say the least, be politically complex and require immense support from many quarters. Still, at a time of major healthcare challenges across the country, the union can at least point to its advocacy as a form of action.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, the stats for women composers in Hollywood have not improved. Just eight of this year’s top 100 grossing films feature original scores by women; the past two years have seen percentages between 7 and 9%, all down from 14% in 2023.

In a recent development, but female composers continue to be in the awards conversation, and not all for their music. Laura Karpman, composer of “American Fiction” and the current Netflix miniseries “East of Eden,” has entered her first film as director in the documentary short subject category: “Cosmic Symphony.” Related Stories Trump Advisor Steven Paul Hopes U.S. Tax Credit Will Be 'Active' in January, Tariffs Are Old News: ‘Now It’s All Hands on Deck Federal Credit’ Bill Maher Mocks ‘GTA 6’-Playing Young Men With Awful ICE Joke.

The film is a timely look at four musical artists who lost priceless, beloved instruments in the Palisades and Eaton fires of January 2025: composer Starr Parodi, whose 1928 Steinway piano was heard in dozens of MGM scores including “The Wizard of Oz”; songwriter Diane Warren, who lost a Yamaha grand; jazz bassist John Clayton, whose string bass was nearly 200 years old; and Altadena educator Susie Chung, whose brown Steinway was played by Lady Gaga in “A Star Is Born” and on the 2019 Oscarcast.

Recent findings suggest that “I believe my piano has a soul… I have a little regret that I left her alone,” Chung states in the film, and that sentiment is echoed by the other musicians. “Instruments have hearts, they have souls, they have lives,” says Warren, a 17-time best song nominee. Two days before the fires, Warren was filmed performing her Oscar-nominated song “The Journey” on the piano in her Malibu beach house.

Clayton’s bass, once owned by the legendary Ray Brown, had accompanied Ella Fitzgerald, Frank Sinatra, Nat King Cole and Duke Ellington. Recalling its past, he mentioned “that bass and the music that it made was bigger than any of us could ever be.”.

Parodi describes her lost keyboard as having “this beautiful, haunting, bell-like sound… warm and thick,” and she tells the harrowing story of watching her house go up in flames via their doorbell camera and later unearthing the remains of her MGM piano in the rubble.

Recent findings suggest that thousands of instruments were reduced to ash during the L.A. fires. “I felt it was a story that was really important to be told,” Karpman states. “When you live with these instruments, they have personalities, they see history.”.

Sources indicate that in addition to the interviews and performance footage, she added lively, colorful animation to the story. Animator Tempe Hale sought “to make the instruments come alive again, (to convey) the kind of fun and glory and energy that these instruments have.”.

Karpman also composed the score for her film, incorporating both orchestral and choral sounds to suggest the music still being made, in the beyond, by those lost music makers.

Scottish composer Anna Meredith wrote one of the year’s most unusual scores for the romantic fantasy “Wicker,” which stars Olivia Colman as a fisherwoman and Alexander Skarsgård as her artificial husband, made for her by a basket weaver in their medieval village.

Industry observers note that the entire score is played by just four people: a violist, a cellist, a recorder player and Meredith herself. “I’d much rather start small with a tiny lens, and see what you can do with it, rather than have every sound in the world, where it could just sound like any old thing. You have to really think creatively,” she says.

Directors Alex Huston Fischer and Eleanor Wilson reached out to Meredith during shooting (to write music for a wedding scene), and she swiftly became part of a team that included several women in key roles (including editor Sofi Marshall). The composer decided that the timeframe and the nature of the story demanded wooden instruments for a “timeless quality.”.

Meredith used as many as 10 different recorders, “from tiny little baby ones, only 20 centimeters; lots of ones in the conventional treble tenor range; and some bonkers instruments, including a bass one and a contrabass one which was so tall we had to move to a different recording studio. We had to find one with a skylight to fit the neck of that one, like seven feet tall.”.

According to recent reports, the recorders represented the fisherwoman and her wicker husband, while the strings (the darker sounds of viola and cello) represented the villagers. “It’s not nice string sounds,” she says, “it’s slithery, nasty sounds. Their sound worlds are, initially, kept quite different, and then the strings sort of ‘infect’ the recorders as the villagers start to impose on their relationship.”.

The directors “wanted the score to be bold,” Meredith adds, “and it’s loud as well. The music is upfront. I’m very proud to be part of a film with a strong female story and so many important female elements, both on and off the screen, that have been part of it.”.

Sources indicate that for “Tenzing,” the untold story of the Nepalese-Indian Sherpa who accompanied Edmund Hillary to the top of Mount Everest in 1953, Norwegian-born, Stockholm-based composer Rebekka Karijord insisted on cultural authenticity. “I felt, early on, that we needed to have a collaboration with Nepalese musicians that isn’t like an exotic tone or a color,” she says. “It had to be a deep collaboration.”.

She enlisted a Nepalese spiritual leader and Buddhist nun, Ani Choying Drolma, to contribute traditional Buddhist chants; Nepal’s premier flautist and throat singer Manose Singh; and actress Thinley Lhamo, who plays Tenzing’s wife Dawa in the film and is also a highly regarded singer of Tibetan opera.

Sources indicate that lhamo “has the most amazing voice,” Karijord claims. That voice becomes, in a sense, the sound of the mountain itself. “I wanted to have something that could transcend the physical effort, that could pull us into the spiritual aspect, and her voice really solved that for me throughout the score.”.

In addition, she had the sound team record a number of unique sounds from the region—yak bells, goat bells, the sound of prayer wheels in the temples, Tibetan singing bowls and gongs—which she and her percussionist sampled and added to her musical library for incorporation into the score.

The film details England’s drive to be the first nation to reach the summit of the world’s tallest peak, Karijord points out. “It needed the big cinematic muscles, a meeting between Western and Eastern. If I could make the mountain, this goddess, beautiful and pristine and dangerous and magnetizing, then we will understand why’re drawn to her—both Tenzing as a little boy growing up at the foot of the mountain, and these Englishmen wanting to conquer it.”.

Karijord employed a 40-piece string section from the London Contemporary Orchestra, in part to convey the danger of crevasses, avalanches and rumbles in the ice, along with a handful of woodwind and brass players and a 12-voice choir. Textural elements, such as the sound of breathing, also became a factor in the score.

Sources indicate that regarding the few female composers scoring studio films, Karijord notes that “it’s such a deeply empathetic craft to score films, and it’s a deeply collaborative craft. I know a lot of women who are both very empathetic and collaborative and brave. So I think there should be more of us doing it.”.

Alexander Zverev misrepresented the result of his 2024 domestic abuse trial, causing harm to his former partner and the mother of his child, Brenda Patea's lawyer has told DW.

The case ended without a verdict after both sides reached an out-of-court settlement. Zverev, who won the French and US Open in 2026, is alleged to have told French publication L'Equipe that: "I did everything I could, and my innocence has been proven.".

As Zverev's lawyers noted in a statement sent to DW: "The criminal proceedings were discontinued... without any finding of guilt, and the presumption of innocence remains unaffected.".

However, Zverev's statement has harmed Patea's standing and her career as an influencer, according to her lawyer, Michael Scheele.

Recent findings suggest that "What she suffered after this interview in L'Equipe was published is nothing but a shitstorm. It's also detrimental to her business," Scheele told DW.

"We still don't know the truth objectively and we have an agreement in which he committed not to talk about the incident and the case at all," he added.

In a recent development, however, in the statement sent to DW, Zverev's lawyers asserted that "there has been no breach of any contractual obligations or violation of Ms. Patea’s personality rights.".

Sources indicate that zverev had made similar comments before. On the day the settlement was reached, the tennis pro spoke to reporters at the 2024 French Open.

"That's what dropping the case is: That is innocence. They're not going to drop the case if you're guilty at the end of the day," he said.

The lawsuit, seen by DW, states that Zverev should be subject to "a fine of up to €250,000 ($275,000) to be determined for each instance of violation — and, in the event that such fine cannot be collected, substitute custodial detention of up to six months," should he be found guilty.

Zverev's lawyers reject the allegations.

According to recent reports, "Our client will defend himself against the lawsuit. If the statement attributed to him was indeed made in the form alleged, we consider it to be a permissible expression of opinion protected by Article 5(1) of the German Basic Law," they noted.

According to recent reports, "Our client would merely have expressed his personal conviction that he had done everything in his power to refute the allegations made against him and that he considers his innocence to have been confirmed by the outcome of the criminal proceedings. "He is fully entitled to hold and express this view.".

The law firm, Schertz Bergmann, added that: "Unlike the opposing counsel, we intend to conduct these proceedings in court rather than in the press.".

Scheele said he and his client did not want to go back to court but were frustrated in their efforts to resolve matters in other ways.

"We went forward writing to him in a polite way, asking him to sign and to declare that he's not going to repeat what he said. And he didn't reply. So we wrote twice more, no reply.

"That's when we had to decide to go to court, which was not the aim at the beginning. We wanted to avoid it, but we had no other choice.".

Zverev, now resident in Monaco, is currently playing in the season-ending ATP Finals tournament in Turin.
